item.title: Recapping the Yankees’ low-minors seasons
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: The minor-league season has officially come to an end, a season in which we saw a bit of a shift from the usual trend of Yankees’ minor league seasons.We didn’t see too many midseason departures due to a weird deadline, we didn’t see a plethora of starting pitchers excel and we saw, for once, a group of hitting prospects that actually showed promise. Remember, entering this year, the No. 4 hitting prospect in the organization behind George Lombard Jr., Dax Kilby, and Spencer Jones was… who, exactly?Scott will have you covered in the coming days with a Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders-intensive recap, but here’s the final evaluation of the rest of the full-season affiliates in a player-specific format, where I highlight some of the players to watch who defined the seasons at their respective levels.Double: The hitter with the best name brand here, Avina had a solid season all around in his first season in Double-A, but warts still remain. Acquired in the Jake Bauers trade after 2023 (who would’ve thought he’d turn into in Milwaukee), Avina was remarkably consistent all year through late July, even winning Eastern League Player of the Month after posting a 1.106 OPS in May. However, as has been his bugaboo at times in his career, he ended the season in a slump, hitting just .229 with a 90 wRC+ in his final 41 games. It might’ve been the result of a midseason approach change, as he cut down on strikeouts at the expense of power production. When he was raking during the early summer, he was striking out nearly 30 percent of the time. He should get to Triple-A at some point next year, but I’m not convinced he’s passed all the tests to get there yet.: Somerset’s MVP in 2026, the corner infielder was a 20/20 bat this year at the level, showing a side of him that we hadn’t quite seen. The 2023 18th-round pick out of Washington started his professional career with extremely little pop, but has slowly tapped into his raw power over the course of his career. Now finishing his age-24 season, Morales was reliable all season long in Somerset.He finished slashing .282/.372/.479 with a 129 wRC+ while splitting time at first and third base. I’m not entirely sure of his big league projectability, but this is a guy who will be in Scranton next year. With 156 total games of Double-A experience, it’s time to see if he can sink or swim.: There were a few quiet minor-league free agent signings who fared pretty well for the Yankees this year. Gladney is one of them, posting a 113 wRC+ in Double-A after spending six years in the White Sox organization. We’ll see if he re-ups on another minor league deal or heads elsewhere. Every draft, the Yankees pick one guy who displayed big-time power in college and see if it translates. It doesn’t usually work, and it seemed like Moylan would be the latest example of the archetype failing in the pros… but maybe there’s something there. After struggling to hit much of anything through 2025, the 24-year-old finally got on a heater down in High-A before a late June promotion. After being called up, he posted a 118 wRC+ in 68 games in his first taste of Double-A. His 29 home runs were the most in the farm this year. Keep an eye on him. Through late June, the closest catching prospect to the majors in the system was one of the worst hitters in the entire system, but he suddenly found something when the calendar flipped to August. After hitting one singular homer in his entire pro career through June 30th, he had six in July. In his final 150 plate appearances, he slashed .319/.351/.521. I’d have him repeat the level to see if those two months were a fluke or a sign of things to come.Garrett Martin, Tyler Hardman, Marco Luciano: A grab bag of guys you’ll hear about from Scott in his Scranton roundup. These three guys were part of a historic start to the season for the Patriots, combining for 44 home runs in 550 plate appearances. Hardman hit a wall in Triple-A, the erstwhile Giants prospect Luciano did incredibly well and should push for a 40-man spot this offseason, and Martin suffered a season-ending injury in July. It’s a real shame; he was on pace to go well past 30/30 this season. Just a really disappointing season from the former first-round pick. He had a 4.45 ERA in 56.2 innings, struggling with a high walk rate despite having stretches of brief brilliance with his enticing stuff. The injuries were rough, costing him a month early in the year and leaving him with a summer of building back up. Just a few weeks after finally getting back to full strength, he was put on the 60-day injured list. Next year will be big for him.: This was Somerset’s best pitcher all season. In 81.1 innings, the former 16th-round pick pitched to a 3.65 ERA with a 22.0 K-BB%, boasting one of the largest strikeout rates of any Double-A pitcher by leaning heavily on his filthy secondaries. He hit a major wall in Triple-A and will have to fine-tune some things to avoid being the next Edgar Barclay with his low-90s fastball, but it was a step forward for a guy who has a case to be the org’s Minor League Pitcher of the Year. If it’s not Rivas, it might be Fox. The Notre Dame product had a really strong debut season, tossing 130 total innings across two levels. What might be most impressive? After being so-so in Hudson Valley, he was aggressively pushed to Somerset in late July and excelled, pitching to a 3.97 ERA in eight starts across 47.2 innings. This guy eats innings like a bowl of cereal in the morning. Not related to the Guardians’ closer, Smith had some prospect stock entering the season, but is likely off everyone’s boards after struggling to a 5.27 ERA in 124.2 innings. The 24-year-old former sixth-round pick will repeat the level in 2026 looking to find the stuff that had him jump up prospect lists in A-ball a few years ago. A former Astros prospect acquired last July, Austin was Somerset’s closer in 2025, but had to repeat the level this year. I thought he might be able to break through into Scranton this year, but he battled some early struggles to make his season numbers more palatable towards the end, as the 25-year-old finished with a 3.61 ERA in 57 innings. He earned a late-season promotion to Scranton for his exceptional work down here this season. When he was drafted, he sat 91-92. Now, two years after Tommy John surgery? How about 96-98? Command is still a bit of an issue, but he struck out 67 in 41.2 effective innings at this level this season. The Yankees love to play with overage undrafted free agents with outlier traits in the bullpen. Rossi is quite old for a guy who made his pro debut last summer, but the 26-year-old has been exceptional at keeping the ball in the ballpark (3 HR allowed in 94 career innings) and racking up strikeouts. He had a 27.0 K-BB% in the minors this year while not allowing many homers and a .171 BAA. That’s not bad.High-A Hudson Valley RenegadesIt was a strong debut season for Jackson, who battled a few minor ailments (three different injured list stints) to have one of the more productive all-around seasons in the system, slashing .262/.360/.459 with 41 stolen bases in 101 games across two levels, being promoted in early August to Somerset. He spent much of the season at shortstop, but should settle at second or third base long term. The former fifth-round pick is in a good spot to be a featured face in Somerset in his age-23 season next year. Remember me? The former uber-prospect revived his stock after a miserable two years in Tampa and a dreadful first two months in Hudson Valley, with an exceptional finish to the season, slashing .305/.377/.521 with a 133 wRC+ in his final 83 games across two levels. He’s still extremely athletically gifted and just turned 22 years old. He popped some big exit velocities and displayed tremendous arm strength, splitting time at shortstop and third base this year. He has a toolkit; let’s keep an eye on him next year. Is this the new best catching prospect in the system? Hard to say. Genther, a former outfielder from Rhode Island, converted to catcher after signing as an undrafted free agent last summer and spent this season as a work in progress on both sides. He bounced back from a putrid start (0 HR in first 40 games) to ultimately finish as the Renegades’ best hitter, and should get to go to Somerset next year. Now, he is an extreme work in progress behind the plate, allowing a truly baffling number of stolen bases (196 in 65 starts). You don’t hear of many players coming from Puerto Rico anymore because of how their pipeline has changed over the years, but Rodriguez is the organization’s most notable Puerto Rican as a former 17th-round pick. He was a pretty niche prospect for his entire career, but got hot in June (.319/.396/.615) to put himself on the map. He unfortunately suffered a season-ending injury in late July, but having just turned 22, there’s time for him to become someone. : Another former undrafted free agent, McCann split time across three different levels this year, but never stopped displaying his raw power. The 22-year-old from Virginia Tech slugged .544 in the first 68 games of his pro career and also saw time at first base this season. He’s a fun prospect. A six-game cameo in Tampa last year got a lot of people excited about the Missouri alum’s potential, but the former 16th-round pick looked like one for much of the season, with big contact issues delaying a seemingly overdue promotion to this level. After he got to Hudson Valley? He stepped up his game, reining in those whiff issues and rediscovering his unique power-speed combo. He finished with 24 home runs and 41 stolen bases, the first Yankee to reach those numbers in 32 years. For much of this season, a guy who’s been hyped as one of the organization’s best pitching prospects looked pretty tough. He was able to routinely go deep into games, but he struggled with command and missing bats, posting a single-digit K-BB% all season long. Due to the roster churn and promotions, he got a late promotion to Somerset and actually finished really strong, posting three consecutive starts of at least six innings with 21 total strikeouts to zero walks. It was also nice to see him build up to 105 innings after his injuries last year. The stuff is absolutely there for Facundo to be in the big leagues one day; it’s just not going to be as a starter. The Yankees finally got him out of Tampa in April and he showed he can stay healthy, but he wasn’t able to show he can consistently throw strikes. The 24-year-old walked 71 batters in 99 innings in Hudson Valley, but also struck out 123. He should probably be put in the bullpen next year and sent to Somerset to expedite his high-level stuff. Entering this season, you could lump Serna in a group with Henry Lalane as damaged goods after years of injuries, but the 22-year-old found an unlikely revival in 2026, just by finally being able to stay healthy. He blew past his prior career high of 69.1 innings to toss 118.2 and set the Hudson Valley single-season strikeout record at 140, while reasonably managing his walks. The ERA was still pretty average at 4.32 in 23 starts, but he’s back on the prospect radar after vanishing following a brilliant 2021 and 2022.45.1 IP, 3.18 ERA, 3.18 FIP, 1.28 WHIP, 16.3 K-BB%41.2 IP, 3.67 ERA, 4.44 FIP, 1.49 WHIP, 10.5 K-BB%44 IP, 3.48 ERA, 3.78 FIP, 1.32 WHIP, 19.0 K-BB% 51 IP, 2.82 ERA, 3.84 FIP, 1.24 WHIP, 16.1 K-BB%35 IP, 3.86 ERA, 4.36 FIP, 1.14 WHIP, 25.4 K-BB%: It was a lost season for Kilby, who missed several months due to recurring hamstring issues. This was a guy who had skyrocketed into the Top 100 lists entering the season, but only managed 154 plate appearances due to an exceptionally low start. The only two things I really got out of his season? He’s absolutely not a shortstop down the road (second base, third base, or center field seem more likely), and he has one of the best eyes of any 19-year-old I’ve ever seen. He had a 25.3-percent walk rate this season. The Arizona Fall League awaits.: I will try to not be a prisoner of the moment, but this might be the best prospect in the system. A 6-foot-4 athletic freak from the D.R., Pena is just 18 years old and hit historically well in the DSL, becoming the first Yankee in nine years to skip the GCL/FCL and go straight to full-season ball, where he barely slowed down. He finished the season hitting over .350 with truly alien exit velocities for a player his age, strong defense in center field (with a cannon for an arm), and plus-plus speed. This is the most tool-heavy guy in the entire system and I am super excited about 2027 for him.: Who had the best overall numbers for this elite Tampa offense? It was actually Luis Escudero, who slashed .288/.455/.556 in 202 plate appearances after spending the spring at the complex. The 20-year-old packs a lot of pop in a small, 5-foot-8 frame, and somehow managed to have an even better eye than Kilby this year. There wasn’t enough sample to have him go to High-A to start next season, but he’ll be there soon if he continues to produce.: Do you miss Jesus Rodriguez in the system? Here’s your new favorite prospect. Puello is basically a baby Rodriguez, already having experience at catcher, first base, left field, and right field. I’m not sure what his long-term position is, but if any organization can get this guy catching in order, it’s this one. His bat also looks great, smacking 14 home runs in 73 games with some solid game power. : In the most recent edition of “former multi-million prospect shows life,” Mayea looked really bad to start the season, but found something over the course of the regular season. I’m going to need to see a lot more to be truly convinced the 20-year-old is on the right path, but he hit .298 across his final 47 games. Now if he could only find the power… Way too little sample for much on any of these guys. Here’s a sampler:Tyce Armstrong, the guy who once hit three grand slams in a game, carried that Big 12 power into Single-A, finishing the season on an absolute heater.Anthony Potestio, the 11th-round pick, is getting a lot of buzz for how well he handled Single-A pitching as someone who didn’t play in the SEC or Big 12. In 19 games, he slashed .333/.513/.684.Paul Gutierrez-Contreras II has been the most impressive in terms of exit velocities. He’s pumped out a handful of batted balls over 105 mph already. A 2025 undrafted free agent, Boudreau came out of nowhere to be one of the most productive starting pitchers in the system. In 103 innings, he posted a 3.41 ERA with a 17.3 K-BB% and even struck out six in 3.1 shutout innings in a brief Somerset cameo. This is a guy who will have an opportunity to get himself on the map in Hudson Valley next year. Mr. Consistency. West started the season with some growing pains, but ended it as the most effective starter in the system. The 22-year-old finished the season by pitching to a 2.23 ERA across his final 10 starts, averaging six full innings per start. He just got better and better over the course of the season. Oh boy. Mac Heuer suffered a season-ending injury in July. Thatcher Hurd started the season recovering from Tommy John surgery, made eight solid starts, and finished the year injured. Brennan Stuprich spent several months on the injured list. J.T. Etheridge was also only limited to 13 starts, but he finished the season extremely strong and will be a sneaky pitcher to watch in the AFL next month. 47 IP, 2.87 ERA, 4.03 FIP, 1.13 WHIP, 19.3 K-BB% 38.2 IP, 3.49 ERA, 3.77 FIP, 1.32 WHIP, 12.6 K-BB%43.2 IP, 2.47 ERA, 3.73 FIP, 1.12 WHIP, 19.6 K-BB%31.1 IP, 3.73 ERA, 4.22 FIP, 1.76 WHIP, 14.8 K-BB%

item.title: Colapinto handed Sepang penalty for causing Baku F1 pile-up
Why Verstappen says 0.196s Baku finish-line gap to Russell is slightly misleading
Shock inaction over Baku's other F1 team-mate clash explained
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: The intra-team Racing Bulls collision at Formula 1’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix that wiped out Liam Lawson was surprisingly dismissed as needing no further action. Franco Colapinto was handed a 10-second time penalty (converted into a five-place grid drop for the Malaysian Grand Prix) for spearing into his Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris’s McLaren, but the stewards decided not to act on the collision that took place behind them. While Ocon and Lawson were side-by-side in the Turn 1 braking zone, Lindblad ended up locking his brakes and running into Lawson in the sister car, punching a big hole in its floor and ruining Lawson’s race.Within 20 minutes of the incident occurring, the incident had been noted, placed under investigation and then dismissed as needing no further action. Asked about the ruling by The Race, Lawson said: “Great for the team [Lindblad went on to finish seventh], yeah, obviously I'm not going to go and protest my team-mate - but I don't understand it because I got hit so hard that it put a hole in my floor.“I was just turning for the corner, giving the guy space. So where I'm sitting, I don't understand, but let's say it's great for the team.” Lindblad apologised to Racing Bulls and Lawson for the clash but offered two mitigating circumstances for the incident. “It was an absolute mess. I think as you see on almost all safety car restarts here in Baku it gets quite chaotic in Turn 1, I don't know what was happening at the front, but it was pretty poorly managed in the sense that the field wasn't bunched up,” Lindblad said. “From where we were, me and Esteban, we'd gone - or Ollie [Bearman] - about three times on the straight; we'd sort of gone and braked and gone again. So it was complete chaos, the battery wasn't in a good window because of that. “Everyone braked a little bit too late in Turn 1 and I was going to make the move on Esteban and he moved in the last minute - basically moved under braking, so [I] had to take avoiding action, which meant I locked the front slightly and I hit Liam. “So obviously I've apologised to him already; I've apologised to the team because it's not something you want, because there could have been two of us in the points today, but also at the same time we take the result.” Lindblad was speaking fresh from finishing the race with limited time to review the incident, but he says it was “terrible” in the middle of the train at the safety car restart. “It wasn't a well-done restart. In the end it should be a bunched-up field that goes slowly, and then we all go at once,” Lindblad said.“So I'm sure it will get raised at the briefing next week, and it's something we'll discuss, but honestly both restarts weren't very good. “You're trying to look a few cars ahead to see what's going on, but there are so many things we're having to manage here. In the end, it's a 2km straight, tyres are cold, brakes are cold, batteries are obviously a new problem. When everyone's going-and-stopping it's pretty dangerous and I think we need to understand why.” His first mitigating factor, a tricky restart on cold tyres and brakes, is certainly relevant, but whether that should absolve him of any penalty is highly questionable. Those were also factors applicable for the penalised Colapinto, after all. As for Ocon moving under braking, this really doesn’t appear to be the case, with Ocon holding his line to the left of Lawson. If anything, it’s Lawson on the right who makes a move across to try to cover Ocon. Lindblad shouldn’t be judged harshly for giving a fresh-from-the-moment opinion, but what’s baffling is why the stewards elected to quickly rule out any punishment for what appeared to be a clear-cut case of one out-of-control driver slamming into another with a misjudged move. Why did it go unpunished? The stewards predominantly didn’t punish Lindblad because they believed the incident to be a direct consequence of the Colapinto/Gasly/Norris shunt ahead.“That incident, together with Colapinto locking his brakes, triggered a braking reaction among the cars immediately ahead of Lindblad,” the stewards’ decision read.“At the same time, Lindblad was positioned between cars on either side. During the corner, Lindblad made contact with Lawson. “Having reviewed the positioning and movement of the cars involved, the stewards determined that the contact was primarily the result of the restricted space available to Lindblad and the chain reaction caused by the incident ahead, rather than any action or error for which Lindblad could be considered wholly or predominantly to blame.”When you review the incident footage, that explanation feels incredibly generous to Lindblad. The Gasly/Colapinto/Norris crash happened far enough up the road that Ocon and Lawson didn’t appear to initiate any meaningful avoiding action before Lindblad went into Lawson. The stewards' report makes no reference to it - but there could also be the unwritten rule of the stewards not judging team-mate collisions as harshly as collisions involving drivers from different teams. As Lawson himself said: “I'm not going to go and protest my team-mate.”Had the stewards opted for a post-race investigation, Racing Bulls would have obviously requested no penalty. But what colour the cars are shouldn’t be a factor when judging these incidents.

item.title: Huge Crash Takes Down Blasi, Vallieres in Women’s Elite Worlds
item.author: Will Tracy
item.content:encoded: The breakout star of the year was a favorite to win the rainbow bands. At least one in the 15-rider pileup exited the race in a neck brace.

item.title: Mass crash shocks peloton during women's road race at World Championships, with defending champion Magdeleine Vallieres and Paula Blasi among affected riders
item.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
item.content:encoded: The elite women's race was affected by a large crash that saw upwards of 15 riders go down with 95km to go at the 180.1km event held at the UCI Road World Championships on Saturday, including defending champion Magdeleine Vallieres (Canada) and Vuelta a España champion Paula Blasi (Spain), who was forced to abandon the race."When the race entered the circuit, it was crazy," Blasi said. "People were taking too many risks. Now, there was downhill, and three girls crashed but were all behind, so it just went over. Typical scratches from the road, not too much pain."148 riders started the race tackling the hilly 180.1km route featuring the closing Mount Royal circuit and eight ascents of the Camillien-Houde climb (2.3km at 6.2%).The incident happened once the peloton reached the second of eight laps, with the riders coming down 12km into the circuit along Rue Saint-Urbain before turning onto Ave des Pins in the first third of the peloton.The crash also included Femke de Vries (Netherlands), Daniela Campos (Portugal), Julia Borgström (Sweden), Carina Schrempf (Austria), Claudette Nyirarukundo (Rwanda), Flora Perkins (Great Britain), Kate Courtney and Grace Arlandson (USA), Marta Jaskulska (Poland), Sigrid Ytterhus Haugset (Norway), Adèle Normand (Canada), Lauretta Hanson (Australia), and Caroline Andersson (Sweden).At the time of the crash, there was a breakaway of two riders that were part of an initial four-rider move in the peloton, including Natalie Quinn (Team USA) and Marte Berg Edseth (Norway), and they still had a three-minute gap.The crash caused major splits in the peloton, with those involved in the incident scrambling to get back on their bikes and chasing to try and close the gaps, including Kim Le Court-Pienaar (Mauritius) and Sarah Gigante (Australia), while Vallieres was left chasing at more than seven minutes back by the time they were partway through the third lap with 80km to go.With visible wounds to her leg and hand, Vallieres abandoned, but not before arriving back at the finish line and waving to the crowds, bloodied, but with a huge smile still on her face as her title defence came to an early end.Canada cycling's chief of sport Sebastien Travers spoke at the finish, but had little information to provide in the way of Vallieres' condition: "She's being evaluated by our doctors, as well as the organisation's doctors, and as soon as we know more, we will provide more information. Travers hadn't yet seen the incident or spoken to the rider, but also said, "I'm hopeful she can rebound fast, and as I said, this is certainly not the last World Championships.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Subscribers get unlimited access to exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: Alpine to consider what action to take after Colapinto crash
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: Alpine will "consider what course of action should be taken" against its driver Franco Colapinto for the "very poor move" that caused a multi-car crash in Formula 1's Azerbaijan Grand Prix.World champion Lando Norris said Colapinto deserved a race ban after the Alpine driver locked up into the first corner at a restart following a safety car period, and wiped out himself, team-mate Pierre Gasly and Norris too.Colapinto described it as a "big mistake" and said he was "out of control" after locking up as soon as he jumped on the brakes.F1's timing system reported a 10-second penalty for Colapinto after the race had finished for causing a collision, which gets converted into a grid drop for the next race instead as he did not finish.The stewards has announced that this will be a five-place drop.Alpine executive advisor Flavio Briatore said: "I want to take time to reflect on it and consider what course of action should be taken, so we can learn from it and avoid such a situation in future."Briatore said Alpine apologises to Norris and McLaren "for ruining their race", which Colapinto had already done himself too."I know that Franco has taken full responsibility for it, as he should; in fact he braked far too late considering the context of the race and the safety car restart," said Briatore."It was a very poor move for a driver of his experience."It is not clear what action Alpine would be willing to take against Colapinto, like benching him for a race itself, or whether it would limit it simply to a warning internally.However, Briatore is understood to be very unhappy with the error, given the impact it has on Alpine's championship fight.Colapinto and Gasly were on course for a double-points finish for Alpine in the race, at least ninth and 10th, which would have cut the gap to Racing Bulls to just six points in the constructors' championship.Instead the incident allowed Racing Bulls to land an unexpected points haul as the chaos cleared a path for Arvid Lindblad - who drove into his own team-mate Liam Lawson at the same restart but avoided a penalty - to finish seventh.This means Alpine now trails Racing Bulls by 15 points in the fight for fifth."Obviously I'm extremely disappointed with the outcome of today's race, knowing we lost valuable points in the championship fight," said Briatore."These sort of incidents shouldn't happen, particularly when we were running well with both cars in point-scoring positions."I feel very sorry for the team and for Pierre who did a great job all weekend."Norris stands alone in believing a full-on suspension is merited.He was a passenger after locking up and other drivers had sympathy for this, with the top-three finishers - George Russell, Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar - all agreeing a ban would be too harsh."It was a small error that had a big consequence," said Russell. "I think, personally, race bans should come from drivers intentionally doing something very dangerous and very reckless."So I think it was unfortunate."Hadjar actually said the track is "not good enough" because it is bumpy off-line and hard to generate tyre temperature behind the safety car.Wiping out two cars, and the call for a ban, conjures images of the 2012 Belgian GP start shunt caused by Romain Grosjean, which he got a one-race ban for.But there are two key differences in Colapinto’s crash – it involved a smaller number of cars, and Grosjean's ban was the trigger for a formal licence penalty point system that now tots up driving offences over a 12-month period.So, there is a structure in place to punish repeat offenders of dangerous or deliberate acts. Which is why unilaterally banning Colapinto would be heavy-handed at best as the system will take care of that if he proves a repeat offender and it is applied correctly.Facing the wrath of a stern operator like Briatore, mourning the loss of an important result in the team's championship fight, is an unenviable punishment in itself. But it could certainly be argued that this sort of crash might have merited a rare application of licence penalty points in addition to a five-place grid penalty.

item.title: Winners and losers from F1's 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: Team-mates colliding, the world champion calling for a driver to be banned, a win drought broken, a top team resurgent and a returnee on the podium - there was plenty going on in Formula 1's 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix.Here's our take on who came out best and worst.Loser: Franco Colapinto After a couple of encouraging signs at Monza - where Franco Colapinto was fast but made errors - and Madring - where Colapinto was quicker than Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly and arguably executed his best weekend yet in F1 - he went and spoiled it all by doing something stupid.A few drivers spoke out in his defence. Carlos Sainz addressed the tricky tyres, dirty circuit and weird power delivery of the engines in Baku, while Arvid Lindblad criticised the way the safety car restarts were handled. But ultimately Colapinto was the only one to lock both front wheels and clatter into two cars at once. When one of those cars is your team-mate's you really are in trouble. He at least took "full responsibility" - not that there was much else he could do in the circumstances.And because he couldn't serve the 10 second time penalty the stewards gave him, that will mean a grid penalty for Sepang. - Ben AndersonFrom looking odds on for a double points finish to actually achieving a catastrophic double DNF in the space of one major Colapinto braking misjudgement. This was ultimately a disastrous conclusion to the weekend for Alpine, after producing what Gasly called "the best race car we've had so far this year".Colapinto wiping out both Gasly and the McLaren of Lando Norris not only robbed Alpine of at least the seven championship points they were holding before it all went wrong, it also created the conditions for Lindblad to bag the seventh place Gasly was holding and extend the gap Racing Bulls holds over Alpine to 15 points in their battle for fifth in the constructors' title race. Winner: Isack Hadjar (3rd)April 21 2024. That's how far you have to go back for Red Bull's most recent double podium before Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar's 2-3 finish in Baku. It's frankly an absurd stat for a team that, despite its troubles, has so obviously remained among F1's top operators throughout that time.This was as good a performance as we've seen from Hadjar since his graduation to the senior team - he acknowledged as much, saying it was the "first time with the team that I actually get to do a very clean weekend" - all the more impressive considering it came on his first weekend back from injury.He was effective in battle, understood the assignment when Verstappen closed up to him, and played the team game like a pro. Even the radio messages felt like they were a little less terse than usual here.If he was looking to show Red Bull what it had been missing while he was out, this was a damn good way to do it. Loser: McLaren (14th and DNF)Turn 1 felt as if actively malicious to the McLarens this Saturday, with two offs and one crash that meant zero points on a weekend the team really should have outscored the power-limited Ferraris.Norris seemed up against it (speed-limited by an issue but also clearly just in a bit of a funk) throughout the entirety of the weekend, so took the crash with the Alpines - shortly after he'd messed up his own race already by visiting the run-off at the same corner - as a final insult to cap off a miserable outing.He was unsparing in his assessment of Colapinto's error, but also just unhappy about his race."I had no chance out there with the speed I had," he lamented. "Sure there were some things I wasn't doing well enough in driving and I need to see what I could improve next time, but at the same time, the speed that they came past me, that was impossible. So it was a pretty impossible task out there."But team-mate Oscar Piastri was doing stellar work in the fight for a podium until it was undone by a strange lock-up of both fronts that sent him down the order."I didn't think I did anything spectacular [to cause it]," he mused. "Obviously I was on a different line to what I normally would be, defending, so I don't know if I was on a crown in the road or something, but it certainly was a surprise to me." Winner: George Russell (1st)George Russell's victory from pole position, which he described as "the most dominant weekend I've had in my career" validates the progress he's spoken repeatedly about making since the August break. After all, while he was given a clear run by title rival Kimi Antonelli clipping the Turn 1 wall in qualifying, Russell was genuinely quick and looked to have a pace advantage over his Mercedes team-mate anyway."I'm very proud of the resilience that I and my close group of engineers have shown during the tough periods this year, because there's been a lot of hard work to overcome some of the challenges to adapt my driving style to suit this new car better," said Russell. "F1 is so tough you don't get opportunities to practice this."And finally, it's coming to me a bit more intuitively than it once did, and I'm gaining confidence. And especially on circuits like this, it just allows you to eke out that little bit more on the brakes, get that little bit closer to the walls, and it's been a flawless weekend."Loser: Valtteri Bottas (DNF)Fastest race lap is usually a rubbish metric to measure performance in an F1 race, but Valtteri Bottas's being 1.5s down on what Cadillac team-mate Sergio Perez managed does seem reflective of the race we saw.Even before his crash at the end of the race - attributed to a harvesting glitch triggered by an earlier off at Turn 1, as "the systems got a bit confused" - the performance was properly, head-scratchingly miserable."A long one," Bottas admitted. "Just, honestly, no pace at all. I could only fight with Fernando [Alonso]. For sure, we lost some time there, but otherwise just pretty far off, so lots of things to look into from this weekend.""Pretty far off" is an understatement - Bottas was nearly a minute down on Perez at the time of his first pitstop, so whatever was wrong was wrong - and has to be a huge priority for himself and Cadillac to figure out. Winner: Max Verstappen (2nd)This was Verstappen and Red Bull's strongest weekend in terms of pace and the fact he finished just two tenths of a second behind winner Russell despite a power unit disadvantage is proof of the progress Red Bull is making.While his victory chances might have been boosted had he started where he should have done on the front row, instead of eighth thanks to a power unit problem, Verstappen suspects that it would have been difficult to have done better than second anyway. "Even if I started second, I think the pace of George would have been very hard to pass," said Verstappen. But the fact Red Bull was a genuine victory contender in Azerbaijan (a rarity in 2026) and the tantalising possibility that starting where he should have done could have led to victory, is a much-needed boost for Verstappen. After Carlos Sainz was given a five-place penalty having initially qualified in ninth, Alex Albon was given the chance to avenge the defeat from his Williams team-mate, given he was dumped out in Q2.He was keeping Esteban Ocon behind in 13th when he crashed at Turn 3, locking up and heading straight into the wall. Sainz recovered from dropping to 19th with an early stop to come back and score a point.Albon said the incident was "odd". He reckoned a combination of a big wind gust, and the Williams car's characteristic of raising a wheel under heavy braking, could have caused the incident, although he still acknowledged his need to hold his hands up for it.A big opportunity missed, especially to outperform his team-mate, who repeatedly bounced back from adversity this weekend. Winner: Arvid Lindblad (7th)After consecutive crashes in FP2s at the Madring and in Baku, Lindblad was struggling for confidence entering this race, and even though it wasn't the perfect way to do it, leading the midfield and bagging big points in Sunday's race will be a nice boost.First, the elephant in the room, his contact with team-mate Racing Bulls Liam Lawson on the lap 39 safety car restart.Lindblad claimed Ocon "basically moved under braking" so he "had to take avoiding action which meant I locked the front slightly and I hit Liam". Whatever the accuracy of those mitigating circumstances (a review of the angles suggested Ocon wasn't doing so), Lindblad escaped unpunished and inadvertently benefitted from the chaos.He also criticised the slackness of the start and how it was poorly formed up, causing drivers to accelerate then brake repeatedly.After that, he pulled off some epic overtakes in the final stint and capitalised on Ocon's poor run to the line to take seventh by 0.030s.It moves him to within four points of Gasly and a place in the drivers' championship top 10, and extends Racing Bulls midfield constructors' lead by six points to 15. Great recovery. Loser: Audi (11th & 13th)With Alpine having taken itself out of the Azerbaijan GP and McLaren in a world of woe, Baku should have been the perfect opportunity for Audi to bag some decent points.Instead, a major upgrade that arrived for this weekend was not enough to help Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto into the top 10 as Audi lost big ground to closest rival Haas.The lost opportunity owed a lot to its Achilles' Heel: a lack of engine power. It's struggled all season with it and it left both drivers unable to do much on Saturday.Bortoleto typified the situation when he said the Audi was "flying" in sector two, but was all at sea on the run across the start-finish line."On the straights, we were super slow," he said. "I was leaving the last corner, I think, 0.2 seconds from Liam for like five laps, and I couldn't overtake him at the end of this straight. I couldn't be closer than that!" A bittersweet return to the points here for Haas?Perhaps, considering Ocon's final-straight defeat in the fight for seventh place with Lindblad, in part a consequence of Ocon backing off after cutting the corner passing Bottas's Cadillac and 'overdoing' said bit of backing off.But neither Ocon nor ninth-place finisher Ollie Bearman seemed to mind too much at the flag. This is just a third points finish of the year (and a best to date) for Ocon who, in the week where it emerged he is heading for the Haas exit, said of his result "I deserved that, not all the rest of this year".The relief was palpable for Bearman, too, as he ended an even longer wait for points that had stretched back to the Canadian GP in May.And beyond the breaking of those point-less streaks, and the six-point gain on an Audi team that somehow failed to score, don't underestimate the significance of Haas finally getting two cars into broadly the same competitive window - and being able to reap rewards for doing so. Loser: Aston Martin (2x DNF)Aston Martin's upgraded chassis and Honda power unit was supposed to have turned the corner on its season – but Azerbaijan proved to be another race to forget.Both cars retired – Lance Stroll out early with a water pressure problem while Fernando Alonso's exit came after what he described as a mysterious power loss down the straight that was costing him 1.5-seconds alone (Honda said no engine issue has been identified as it stands).The race trouble came after little sign of promising pace all weekend, as the deficits in the Aston Martin package remained obvious. Stroll bemoaned it simply as a lack of downforce and a lack of power.For Alonso, who continues to weigh up his F1 future, it is fairly clear where step forward has got to come from."When we press the throttle pedal, when we go on the straight, we need to rely on Honda getting better and better," he said."We made a step forward this year with the engine upgrade, but obviously, as we see, there is not enough, and we need to keep on going."

item.title: Norris says Colapinto should be banned after accident
item.content:encoded: World champion Lando Norris calls for Alpine's Franco Colapinto to be banned for causing an accident at a restart at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

item.title: Briatore to reflect on necessary action after Colapinto's "poor" Baku blunder
Saturday Posted & Toasted Notes: KAT talks, falling stars, camp decisions, life choices
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: Back-to-back daily Notes posts are all you need to know to start believing the season is right around the corner, starting with Monday’s media day. Can’t wait!Karl-Anthony Towns’ contract situation remains the biggest storyline entering Knicks training camp. SNY’s Ian Begley reported the Knicks and Towns have remained in regular contact throughout the offseason, with discussions described as positive and the organization making clear it wants Towns in New York long term. However, no agreement is imminent.Salary-cap expert Yossi Gozlan told Begley that extending Towns, Hart and McBride while also planning for future Jalen Brunson and OG Anunoby extensions will require difficult financial decisions unless the salary cap rises faster than projected or James Dolan changes his stance on going over the second apron.ESPN’s Brian Windhorst and Tim MacMahon believe the two sides remain far apart financially, with the former saying there’s “tens of millions” separating them and MacMahon suggesting the gap could even be eight figures annually.The Knicks’ final roster spot remains one of training camp’s biggest competitions, with Begley expecting veterans Bruce Brown, John Konchar and Ochai Agbaji to battle for a wing spot while Drew Eubanks and James Wiseman compete for the reserve center role. Unless New York sheds salary in a trade (looking at you, Paco), only of those five veterans is likely to make the standard roster.Keeping it Begley, the pundit also expects rookie Tyler Nickel to receive one of the remaining camp spots and believes Kevin McCullar will eventually earn a place on the roster as well.Jalen Brunson shared the defining moment that shaped his basketball career during an appearance on the “Things No One Tells You” podcast. His parents told him he could only choose two of three priorities: school, basketball, or a social life. You know what happened next.Salty ESPN “analytics pioneer” Dean Oliver isn’t buying the consensus on Brunson’s standing among the league’s elite. While ESPN’s Top 100 panel ranked Brunson No. 6 overall, Oliver said his statistical models place the Finals MVP “around the No. 25 range” and argued New York media attention inflates public perception.“I love Brunson’s game, but his lofty ranking benefitted not only from recent bias but also from the New York media bias. (That bias might also help you forget that Brunson missed the shot in the most iconic image from the Finals, when OG Anunoby swooped in for the putback game-winner to clinch Game 4.)“The metrics place Brunson around the No. 25 range heading into the season. That’s not a huge gap. He’s elite, just not No. 6 — at least not during the regular season.”Stephen Curry has agreed to a two-year, $116 million extension with the Warriors that includes a player option for the 2028-29 season. Curry, set to turn 39 midseason, still had one year left in his deal, meaning he could get to complete a nicely rounded 20-season career in The Bay if he retires at the end of his next pact.Greg Oden admitted he never expected to be selected ahead of Kevin Durant in the 2007 NBA Draft and actually wanted to return to Ohio State.North Macedonia great Pero Antić can only joke about making the Rising Stars Challenge at age 31. “I was already a falling star. Everyone was laughing, including my mom and dad.”

item.title: Message in a bottle? Belgium get around lack of radios at World Championships with unique strategy
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: The UCI Road World Championships present several unique challenges for teams in that the use of race radios is prohibited, making communication between the team cars and the riders especially difficult in the chaos of a road race. Most teams will send riders back to the cars for advice, but there is limited time to chat when the race is on.Belgium - with favourites for the elite races in Lotte Kopecky for the women and Remco Evenepoel and Wout van Aert in the men's field - have a special method: taping messages to riders' bottles.During the country's pre-race press conference on Friday, their secret 'message in a bottle' strategy was uncovered by 's Renaat Schotte."We tested that on Friday with the under-23," coach Serge Pauwels admitted. "We work with [message boards] like every year, but we also have a different system with the drink bottles figured out."It's not rocket science, is it? But almost every lap, almost every rider takes on a bottle. And in the under-23s it worked well."The strategy won't make a massive difference for Belgium, Pauwels says, "But it's a good way to get changing situations across to the riders."The atmosphere was so light that thought it must be a joke, with Van Aert laughing, saying, "It's been around for a long time, huh, although I've never raced like this before. For me, it will be new. I will be happy if I will be a little more aware of the race conditions. I'm not a fan of racing without earpieces. I have said that many times." happened to get wind of the team's methods after a labelled bidon was picked up by one of the television cameramen.Now that their secret has been exposed, Van Aert joked, "Maybe we should agree on a coded language."Or maybe we should write true messages on the even laps and false instructions on the odd ones," Pauwels joked."It's just a shame we still have to think about this. I think it was decided at the time to race without earpieces because the races were boring at the time, but that has changed."Evenepoel agreed, saying there are risks to the team's strategy. "If you miss a bottle and there is an important message on it, you have not seen it. It still needs fine-tuning ... But it's a pretty good idea. There are 12 laps and therefore 12 chances to take such a bottle. The chance that we won't know the message is fairly small."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Top 10 F1 closest finishes
Yankees Birthday of the Day: Bobby Shantz
item.author: Nick Power
item.content:encoded: “But it turned out awful nice, I’ll tell you that — 16 years. You know, I lasted more than I thought I would. Boy, what a life. I really enjoyed every minute of it. Even when I was horseshit, I still liked it.”As he approached his 100th birthday in 2025, Bobby Shantz took the opportunity to reflect on his career in baseball. More than 60 years since he’d hung up his cleats, he still had the mind of a ballplayer, reminiscing about the legends he played with and against with vividness and vibrancy. But he also had the perspective of a man who’d been on a long journey — and was grateful for every stop along the way. September 26, 1925 (Pottstown, PA)1957-60Shantz grew up in the suburbs in Pennsylvania. A small kid (his height peaked at 5-foot-6 as an adult), the young Bobby distinguished himself through pinpoint control and all-around athleticism. After his high school coach refused to let him pitch due to his size, a youth baseball manager saw Shantz working out his curveball and decided to give him a shot on the mound. He joined the Army in 1944 and continued to hone his craft on Army baseball teams while stationed in the Philippines, competing against big-leaguers and building confidence in his ability to go pro.Upon his return to the States, Shantz continued to impress in semipro ball but struggled to find any takers among MLB teams due to his stature. Finally, after a couple of teammates with connections in the Philadelphia A’s organization put in a good word, Harry O’Donnell, a scout with the team, signed him to an A-Ball deal. He immediately impressed, winning 18 games in 28 starts and striking out nearly a batter an inning. The next year, at the age of 23, he made the leap all the way to the big leagues, where he would be managed by none other than Hall of Famer and baseball lifer Connie Mack.In his first three seasons in Philly, the southpaw established himself as a strong contributor, pitching around league average and making his first All-Star team in 1951. But it was the following year that would be Shantz’s campaign for the ages. Seemingly out of nowhere, he emerged as the best pitcher in baseball, winning 24 games, posting a 152:63 K:BB ratio, recording a 2.48 ERA, 9.4 rWAR, and taking home the AL MVP. The career year was aided in part by the use of a knuckleball Mack had forbade him from employing but his new manager, Jimmie Dykes, encouraged.In the ‘52 All-Star Game, Shantz struck out the side in his only inning of work, including punchouts of Jackie Robinson and Stan Musial. His newfound stardom even netted him a guest spot on the Ed Sullivan Show.As is so often the case after a superlative season like Shantz’s ‘52, the pitcher took a step back in the years that followed. As he struggled with injury and inconsistency, he went 13-26 with a 4.42 ERA over the next four years, failing to recapture his peak form on floundering A’s teams as the franchise moved to Kansas City. After the ‘56 campaign, the A’s traded their former MVP to the Yankees as part of a 13-player trade. Shantz was a man reborn, leading all of baseball with a 2.45 ERA in ‘57 and earning his first All-Star berth since his MVP season.Shantz also took home the very first AL Gold Glove for a pitcher, his first of eight such awards earned between both leagues. The man’s legacy as one of the greatest fielding pitchers has never been in question. “I’ll occasionally hear a guy introduce me and say, ‘He was the best fielding pitcher in baseball,’ and I’ll say, ‘No, Bobby Shantz was,’” said Jim Kaat, winner of 16 Gold Gloves himself. “He didn’t win a Gold Glove until ’57. Had they given them out starting in ’50, he would have had 16 or 17 as well.”Shantz made the only World Series start of his long career that October, taking the ball in Game 2 against the Milwaukee Braves. He struggled, allowing four runs (three earned) in three innings, but rebounded well in Game 4, tossing three scoreless innings in relief to keep the Yankees in a game they’d eventually tie up in the ninth.Shantz spent three more years in pinstripes, eventually transitioning to a bullpen role, where he pitched well as a proto-closer. Despite finding his greatest individual success in Philadelphia, Shantz would later recount that his time with the Yankees—who won a championship in 1958 and the pennant in three of his four seasons there—was the most rewarding of his career.After the ‘60 season, the Yankees left him exposed in an expansion draft. Shantz was selected by the Washington Senators, who flipped him to the Pirates. He’d spend the final four seasons of his career in a state of perpetual motion, pitching for five different teams as a trusted reliever. After the ‘64 season, at the age of 39, Shantz retired. The 5-foot-6 non-prospect who was rejected repeatedly at the start of his career had stuck around for 16 years in the big leagues.Shantz retired back to Pennsylvania, where he managed a restaurant and co-owned a bowling alley. In 2010, Pottstown High School renamed their baseball park Bobby Shantz Field in honor of their famous alumnus. As the years have gone on and he’s passed the century mark, Shantz has increasingly become the “oldest living” designee in many areas — oldest living MLB MVP, oldest living A’s player, and on down the line. He’s accepted this status with grace and humor, giving colorful interviews and staying connected to the game he loves.On the occasion of his 101st birthday, we celebrate the oldest living Yankee, Bobby Shantz. We’ll let him take us out in his own words: “I had a great life. Jesus, great life. Boy, I’d like to do that all over again.”See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

item.title: CRO Race: Paul Magnier finally gets his victory on stage 5 with mighty sprint
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: After an unsuccessful four days of action at the CRO Race, Paul Magnier finally got the victory he was searching for on stage 5, benefiting from a perfect Soudal-QuickStep lead-out.With the category 2 Plesivica climb coming in the last 25km of the route, it was far from a simple job for the Belgian team to deliver Magnier to the win, with UAE Team Emirates-XRG pacing hard and several attacks being launched before the summit. But on the downhill run for home in Sveta Nedelja and after some elite work from Soudal-QuickStep, racing was kept all together before the final 4km, with many of the fast men returning.With Magnier sat in fourth wheel, they wound things up for the sprint, with Dries Van Gestel providing the final push. Tim Torn Teutenberg tried to jump the Frenchman with an early surge, but once Magnier opened up, he moved away from all his rivals, celebrating with a roar. It brought his 11th win of the season as 35th as a professional, with Rui Oliveira (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) finishing second and Teutenberg third."I’m very happy to be on the top spot of the podium again! The team did an amazing job today! Their lead-out was spectacular, and all I had to do was open my sprint at the right moment and keep it all the way to the line," said Magnier."I knew the parcours from last year and I was aware it would be hard, because some riders were keen on attacking on the climb, but we controlled and brought back all those moves, managing to keep things together for the finale. In the sprint, I started early, but I was confident I could pull it off. Sunday is another opportunity and we are motivated to fight again for the victory."After the peloton came to the line as a bunch, there were no major changes in the general classification, with stage 3 winner Tobias Svarre (Uno-X Mobility) maintaining his slim lead of four seconds overall on Antonio Tiberi (Bahrain Victorious), and eight seconds on Tim Wellens (UAE Team Emirates-XRG).The race will conclude on Sunday in Croatia's capital city, Zagreb, with another expected sprint stage, where bonus seconds could prove essential in the GC race.Paul Magnier (Fra) Soudal-QuickStepRui Filipe Alves Oliveira (Por) UAE Team Emirates-XRGTim Torn Teutenberg (Ger) Lidl-TrekCarl-Frederik Bévort (Den) Uno-X MobilityDario Igor Belletta (Ita) Polti-VisitMaltaEdoardo Zambanini (Ita) Bahrain VictoriousClément Izquierdo (Fra) CofidisAntonio Tiberi (Ita) Bahrain VictoriousSergi Darder Gari (Spa) Caja Rural-Seguros RGAThomas Pesenti (Ita) Polti-VisitMaltaTobias Svarre (Den) Uno-X MobilityAntonio Tiberi (Ita) Bahrain VictoriousTim Wellens (Bel) UAE Team Emirates-XRGSam Maisonobe (Fra) CofidisAdrien Boichis (Fra) Red Bull-Bora-HansgroheDylan Teuns (Bel) CofidisEmil Herzog (Ger) Red Bull-Bora-HansgroheJohannes Kulset (Nor) Uno-X MobilitySteff Cras (Bel) Soudal-QuickStepAimé De Gendt (Bel) Pinarello-Q36.5Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: 'Mr Horner looking for a job' - Vasseur laments Ferrari distractions
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Ferrari Formula 1 team principal Fred Vasseur says he and his team are being undermined by relentless speculation over his future - and acknowledges "Mr [Christian] Horner looking for a job" as part of this.Vasseur took over from Mattia Binotto at the helm of the Ferrari squad in 2023, but - like under his predecessor - Ferrari still has not been able to break through into genuine F1 title contention. In 2026, a potential grid-best chassis has been neutered by a power unit deficit, which Vasseur again accentuated as the primary factor in his team's cars finishing fourth and sixth this weekend in Baku.The race took place against the backdrop of a recent interview with by ex-Red Bull boss Christian Horner, in which Horner claimed that, in terms of running an F1 team again, there was "only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership".That team was implied to be Ferrari, which Horner described as "the dream" destination and "arguably the sleeping giant of F1".When asked by The Race after the Azerbaijan GP about the noise surrounding his own future and Ferrari's F1 team leadership plans, Vasseur briefly pivoted from his usual jokey-and-deflective tone to make it clear he doesn't appreciate the situation."Ah, we are not working in the perfect serenity," he insisted. "For me firstly, but for everybody in the team. For the media, for 50% of the questions [to be] about this, I think it's a bit of a frustrating situation."We are fighting for P2 in the championship, and at the end of the day, we are all speaking a lot about this, and even for the guys in the garage, to discuss about this, it's the best discussion that we can have."But it is what it is, it's not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job - that everybody knows - everywhere."But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team, to rise them to be motivated, focus on what is better today."Each interview, 25 times a day, we are coming back to this."Vasseur also affirmed his commitment to Ferrari and "the best job in the world" - but also curiously added: "But it is like it is. We have still seven races to go, and I will push until the last corner."On whether he would be open to working with Horner within Ferrari, he joked: "You have to ask my assistant."

item.title: Emerging Swiss star Anja Grossmann split between cheering for home squad and 'biggest idol' Demi Vollering in elite women's road race at Montreal Worlds
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Grossmann turns 19 next year and can soon put away any distaste of "hectic" junior racing as she moves to bigger objectives, namely a two-year road contract to race for FDJ United-Suez and also compete in cyclo-cross with their new Specialized TMRW UCI-registered squad.Even during her post-race press conference on Friday, Grossmann was already thinking about her future teammates, Demi Vollering (Netherlands) and Kate Courtney (USA), both racing for their respective countries on Saturday in the elite women's road race at Montreal Worlds."I'm split in two because I'm Swiss," she said about rooting for compatriot Marlen Reusser, who won a second time trial title last Sunday, or pulling for FDJ trade team riders. "I will cheer for the Swiss for sure because I know how strong they are and how nice they are. I will also cheer for Demi and for everyone from FDJ because Demi is my biggest idol. And also Kate Courtney is one of my biggest idols. It's a dream come true to ride next year for them."In the last two years, Grossmann proved her road versatility by sweeping national titles in the time trial and road race. She also finished on the podium at two stages of Valromey Tour Féminin U19 and fourth at the junior In Flanders Fields [previously Gent-Wevelgem]."FDJ, it's the best team for me to choose because they really also support me now, and they just give me the space to develop my best self, and they don't put any pressure on me," she said. "They also support that I love three disciplines, and that's pretty nice for me. I think that's the best thing that could happen to me, and I'm pretty grateful for that opportunity."In addition to excelling on the road, Grossmann competes in cyclo-cross and mountain biking. She's a junior World Champion on the mountain bike, also winning the European Championships in both 2025 and 2026. The cyclo-cross season is just around the corner, where the former European junior champion can build her talents with a small but mighty squad, the new Specialized TMRW squad."With Fem, as with Anja Grossmann and Kate Courtney, we are also reinforcing our ambition to build a truly multi-disciplinary project, capable of welcoming great champions with their own backgrounds, personalities and ambitions," FDJ General Manager Stephen Delcourt said in a recent statement.While Grossmann came short of a gold medal a second time at these championships, she said she learned a great deal about perseverance, and sounded much more mature than her 18 years."Junior racing is always a little bit more hectic and a little bit more without a clear tactic. I thought [the breakaway of] three was really strong. But maybe we should have worked a little bit more together," she said about getting away on the final two laps with a decisive front trio, who were later caught by two other riders with 2km to go."I wanted to work together, but it was not my decision; I cannot change other girls' minds. It is how it is. I think I learned from last year to don't get so nervous when other girls don't want to work together because I think my four laps or three laps today [Friday], the first ones, were pretty good."It's again a third place, but yeah, I learned [a lot], and I also will [try] to enjoy this one. Also after a week, I try to analyse that with my coach and try to get better and stronger, because you can always learn something from every race." item.title: Team masseur to start World Championships men's road race as Slovakia's only rider after desperate situation
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Alongside the superstars Remco Evenepoel, Mathieu van der Poel and Isaac del Toro on the start line of the World Championships men's elite road race on Sunday will be a surprising entry: Vladimír Kováčik, a masseur for the Slovakian national team.It's been a decade since Slovakian superstar Peter Sagan won the second of his three world titles in a row, and while still not one of the major cycling nations, the situation hasn't turned that bleak since the all-time great's retirement. Slovakia has more than enough talent to be able to field a strong team between the likes of Lukáš Kubiš (Unibet Rose Rockets), Martin Svrček (Soudal Quick-Step) and Matthias Schwarzbacher (EF Education-EasyPost), but a series of events led them to this being the only solution.Their ranking meant they were due to be fielding a four-man team, but between injuries and rider schedules taking priority, they found themselves in an emergency, and a potentially costly one, as not fielding a team could see their national championships drop into the B category for 2027, with a cut to the number of UCI points on offer.Late cancellations left them unable to nominate a replacement, with the window for registration closing on September 11, so they were forced to turn to a member of the support staff to protect the future prospects of Slovakian riders."The only nominated racer [for the women's race], Nora Jenčušová, had to end the season prematurely due to injuries and adverse health conditions. Likewise, the only relevant nominated men - Lukáš Kubiš, Matthias Schwarzbacher and Martin Svrček had to cancel their participation at the last moment," read a post from the Slovakian federation's Instagram."Due to the late cancellation of their participation, it was no longer possible to supplement the nomination adequately. Given the UCI rules and the fact that the World Championships are taking place in Canada, the situation was only possible to be resolved through a member of the Slovak team, who was already on site and met the conditions of the start. At the same time, it is not possible to further include U23 in the elite category of quality racers, because they could lose the opportunity to start in their age category."A 28-year-old masseur for the national team, Kováčik has raced previously, but according to his ProCyclingStats profile, not since 2017. That season he was 32nd in the national time trial championships in Slovakia, and he had raced at Paris-Roubaix juniors the season before that – though he did not finish.In the women's elite road race, they will similarly be fielding only one rider, but the situation hasn't been quite as desperate, with Tereza Kurnická taking the start as Jenčušová's replacement, a multiple-time Slovakian national champion in mountain biking.National coach Jakub Vančo explained the consequences in greater detail, stating how essential the points could be for their goal of qualifying for the 2028 LA Olympics, but made sure to stress that the masseur's entry was nothing more than a "formal representation"."For the national champion, the drop is half, for the second one almost two-thirds. We would count the losses in the hundreds. These points are equal to winning a World Tour stage race, which is beyond our capabilities," Vančo told "So we have to fulfil our obligation to the UCI to have someone compete in the elite races. Moreover, next year will be a qualifying year for the 2028 Olympics."Our participation will only be formal. We will have representation in the form of a person who is here and formally meets the conditions and licenses." Slovakia has performed well throughout the ongoing championships in Montreal, Canada, with top young talent and Visma-Lease a Bike rider Viktória Chladoňová winning the women's under-23 road race and Richard Riška taking eighth in the equivalent men's race. It's the future of these riders and the rest of their developing talent that the decision has been made for."Minimum representation of Slovakia in the Elite category is important in terms of maintaining the ranking and point positions required for future nominations for the World Championships, European Championships and Olympic Games," read the post on the federation's Instagram. "Although such a solution is not ideal and it is not a decision that we would accept easily, in the current situation it is necessary to preserve start possibilities for prospective Slovak cyclists and cyclists, such as Chladoňová, Kubiš, Schwarzbacher, Ungerová, Svrček, Riška, Novák, Andacká and other quality juniors. We therefore believe in understanding this extraordinary situation.""I would like to thank Terka Kurnická and Vlad Kováčik for starting in the elite category. With their participation, we will not lose important points that will be useful to us in the future," said Chladoňová.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: 2027 combined UCI World Championships to include 20 disciplines, including Gravel, with demanding road circuit in Sallanches
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: As the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal, Canada prepare to reach their crescendo with the elite women's and men's road races, the organisers of the next Worlds presented a hugely ambitious project for a combined championships bigger than any in history.Bringing together all of the UCI's disciplines except for cyclo-cross and snow bike, the Haute Savoie combined UCI World Championships will include 20 disciplines from BMX to Trials - bringing in the Gravel World Championships for the first time - and gather some 15,000 athletes from 207 nations to compete for 288 titles.The road races will take place in Sallanches, the site of the 1964 Road World Championships where Eddy Merckx won his first title as an amateur at age 19, and where Bernard Hinault won his world title in 1980. Each race will take place fully on a 13.3km circuit that includes 185m of climbing on the Côte de Domancy, a 2.5 km climb that has an average gradient of 9.4%.There will be no lengthy run-out for the elite riders, just 20 laps of the circuit for an incredibly demanding 265 kilometres with 5,700 metres of climbing for elite men, 12 laps/158.6km and 3,420 metres for elite women and under-23 men, 9 laps for under-23 women and junior men and six laps for junior women.Even the time trials will have a climb. The elite and under-23 time trials are 37.2km with a start and finish in Annecy, encircling Lac d'Annecy and climbing over the Côte de Talloires - a 1.5km climb at 6.5% average - for a total of 265 metres of climbing, while juniors begin in Doussard at the south end of the lake for 20.3km and 202 metres of climbing. In the mixed relay, the men will cover the flat first 16.9km while the women will tackle the climb and 20.3km, making for some interesting tactical decisions.But the championships will be much, much bigger than just road cycling, with three BMX events, Indoor Cycling, Esports, Cycle Speedway (think short-track speed skating on bikes), Gran Fondo, Gravel, five Mountain Bike events (Cross-country, Marathon, Downhill, Enduro and E-Enduro), bike Polo, Pump Track, Para-cycling Road, Track (Junior, Elite, Para) and Trials.The combined event is the brainchild of David Lappartient, who said he originally had the idea to combine the five Olympic disciplines every four years while campaigning to become UCI President. During Friday's presentation of the 2027 Worlds, he explained, "Once [I was] elected ... we said to ourselves: 'Why limit ourselves to five? Why not include our various competitions of the year?'"The journey led to the 2023 Glasgow World Championships with 13 disciplines and, after a chance meeting while on holiday in Châtel that led to Lappartient presenting the awards of a Gran Fondo, he met the president of the province, Martial Saddier."That was the first meeting," Lappartient recalled. "And he said, 'I have a dream. I want to bring back the UCI Road World Championship in Sallanches, where Bernard Hinault won. When can it be?'. I said, 'Look, 2025 is in Africa, 2026 could probably be Montreal - here we are - and in 2027, we set up the combined World Championships, but 2028 is free.""But he said, 'Yes, but we are elected until March 2028 ... Why not 2027, the combined?' [I said], 'It's all the disciplines, you know, it will be like 20 UCI World Championships together.' And he said, "OK, done. I'll take that."The agreement held and one year from now, the 'Cycling Games' will be spread across the province, with Les Gets, a long-time MTB World Cup host, hosting the mountain bike cross-country and downhill. Only track cycling will be outside Haute Savoie. Rather than use the nearby Grenoble velodrome, track cycling events will be held in the Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines National Velodrome outside of Paris.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia.
