item.title: New York Yankees vs. Baltimore Orioles: Ryan Yarbrough vs. Brandon Young
item.author: Andrés Chávez
item.content:encoded: After CC Sabathia’s No. 52 retirement ceremony and a rather forgettable Game 1 of Friday’s doubleheader, the New York Yankees will take the field again and face the Baltimore Orioles in the nightcap. The Bombers already know that they will host the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round, and the O’s are already eliminated from playoff contention.As a result, this is merely a tune-up game for New York, but that’s certainly not insignificant ahead of another edition of their rivalry with the Sox. Brandon Young will take the ball for Baltimore, trying to wrap up a solid year. The 28-year-old followed up his mediocre 57.2-inning cameo last year with a very solid campaign in 2026, with 151.2 frames of a 3.62 ERA, a 4.53 FIP, and 127 punchouts. He is not a star, but did more than enough to win a long-term spot on the O’s staff.The Yankees, with that series against their bitter rivals looming, didn’t announce their starting pitcher for Game 2 of the doubleheader until just about 10 minutes ago. Long reliever Ryan Yarbrough gets the nod for his second start of the season; he last pitched on Tuesday. His only other start of 2026 was the second game of another doubleheader against the Dodgers, when he went 2.2 shutout innings back on July 19th.Yarbrough is obviously not built up length-wise to go deep in this one either, but the expectation is that Will Warren will pitch a couple innings as preparation for the playoffs. He last pitched on Sunday in Arizona. Big things were expected from Warren this season, and while he didn’t exactly develop into an ace, he has been steady as a rock with a 4.02 ERA in 152.1 innings. A team would take that from its No. 5 starter any day of the week. David Bednar, Brent Headrick, and Paul Blackburn can only pitch so much, so Warren could certainly make a positive impact in the ‘pen.Also keep an eye on the bullpen for Alexander Cornielle. A career minor-league signed before the season, the right-hander made 16 starts for Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre and was activated to the big-league roster between games with matinee starter Brendan Beck optioned. If he appears tonight or Sunday, it will be his MLB debut.From this point forward, everything the Yankees do on the field will be with the Red Sox in mind, so don’t expect an all-out effort from those expected to be on the Wild Card Series roster. Indeed, there isn’t a ton of overlap between the Game 1 lineup and the Game 2 starting nine, as the Yankees are avoiding using too many players if possible. Indeed, the Game 1 infield went Paul Goldschmidt/José Caballero/George Lombard Jr./Anthony Volpe from first to third, and Game 2 has Luis García Jr./Jazz Chisholm Jr./Volpe/Ryan McMahon, with Volpe giving Lombard a spell by shifting over to his familiar six for the first time since his early-August demotion. Cody Bellinger tags in for Heliot Ramos in left, while Ramos shifts to right and Amed Rosario takes a seat. Austin Wells will catch and Spencer Jones is the only one starting the same position in both games, in center.: Yankee Stadium – Bronx, NY: 7:30 p.m. ET: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 Gotham Sports App, MLB.tv (out-of-market only)

item.title: Yankees flop after CC Sabathia ceremony, lose to Orioles
item.author: Matt Ferenchick
item.content:encoded: With nothing left to play for on either side, the Yankees vs. Orioles series opener was somewhat overshadowed with the number retirement ceremony for CC Sabathia that took place before the game. The expected bad weather tomorrow forced a doubleheader today and moved the ceremony up to this afternoon as well. The short notice change led to the stands being emptier than anyone would like, but it was still a nice ceremony for the now-forever Yankees’ No. 52. Old friends Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances, and Chris Young joined in the festivities on the field, alongside Sabathia’s family.On the field, things could’ve gone better.Making something of a spot start with the doubleheader and the Yankees planning ahead for the postseason, Brendan Beck started for the Yankees. Not that it was something the Yankees were considering, but Beck didn’t particularly make a case to be a last-second playoff roster addition. In his five innings, he allowed seven runs on six hits and three walks, including two home runs. The bullpen wasn’t particularly lights out following him, allowing the Orioles to build up a big lead.The Yankees’ offense was always going to be up against it considering that fact, but they didn’t do much. Orioles starter Trevor Rogers mostly kept the Yankees in check as Baltimore kept adding on. The Yankees could only plate one run from their eight hits, dooming them to a 10-2 loss in the first game of the doubleheader.On the mound, Beck started things off with a couple scoreless innings. However, Baltimore got on the board in the third. Beck nearly got through the inning again, but issued a two-out walk to Dylan Beavers. That came back to haunt him, as Pete Alonso did a Pete Alonso thing and homered to put the O’s in front.An inning later, Beck loaded the bases after walking two and allowing a single. Christian Franklin then dropped in a single, plating another Orioles’ run. After a force out got a runner at home, Beavers took Beck deep for a grand slam, putting Baltimore well in front.The Yankees got on the board themselves in the bottom of the fourth. Heliot Ramos reached with a triple, aided by center fielder Colton Cowser misplaying the carom off the wall. Amed Rosario followed that with an easy single to score the Yankees’ first run.Baltimore got that run back a short time later, thanks to an outfield miscue of the Yankees’ own. With reliever Yerry De los Santos in for the Yankees, Jeremiah Jackson hit a ball to deep right-center. The ball just got over the glove of Spencer Jones and took a fortuitous bounce past him. Jackson managed to race all the way around and beat the throw home for an inside-the-park homer, the first one in the Bronx in a dozen years — coincidentally with today’s honoree on the mound against Wil Myers. Alonso added a more conventional homer in the seventh in that it went over the fence, but it was unconventional in that it was an absolute bomb, 471 feet away.Honestly, I can’t even be mad at that one. Baltimore would tack on one more run to get to double digits for the game. Paul Blackburn and David Bednar got their work in as expected, and we now won’t see them again until the Wild Card Series.The Yankees did get one run back after Spencer Jones singled in the bottom of the ninth and eventually came around to score on a Paul Goldschmidt sacrifice fly. Ben Rice struck out looking to end it.One pretty disappointing thing to come out of the game was the play of the offense. Yes, the game didn’t actually mean anything, but the Yankees did send out the likes of Goldschmidt and Rosario and their theoretical “lefty” lineup. Them not doing much on offense isn’t what you would want to see considering that the Red Sox Wild Card Series lineup is now locked in and Boston has a bunch of left-handed pitchers they can throw at the Yankees.The second game of today’s doubleheader is set to begin at 7:30pm ET, which New York just announced. Brandon Young will go for Baltimore, while the Yankees will counter with Ryan Yarbrough, with Will Warren expected to provide relief work in anticipation of his playoff role.

item.title: UCI Road World Championships: Alejandra Neira takes junior women's road race title from five-rider escape in Montréal
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Alejandra Neira gave Spain their third gold medal of the UCI Road World Championships, winning the junior women's road race in a hotly-contested five-rider sprint in Montreal.Neira patiently waited until the final 150 metres to put in a massive turn of speed, leaving Matilde Rossignoli (Italy) in her wake to take silver, while Anja Grossmann (Switzerland) claimed third.After the dual titles from Benjamín Noval in the junior men's time trial and road race, Neira's gold medal represents the future of Spanish cycling."I can't believe it. It's the best day of my life," Neira said. "I can't believe that I'm the World Champion. It's incredible."Last year, it was Neira's teammate Paula Ostiz who won the title. Now it's her turn. "Paula is a big, big friend, also teammate, and to be the World Champion after her, wow, incredible."Neira was part of a three-rider escape along with Grossmann and Rossignoli, but the pair were caught in the final three kilometres by Maria Okrucińska (Poland) and Mirthe Mons (Netherlands), which shook her confidence a bit."When the other riders arrived, I lost a little bit my confidence, because Maria is a really good sprinter. But I tried to keep on her wheel, and then when I saw that I have to pass, I went."Grossmann finished fourth in the junior women's time trial, so found redemption with a bronze medal, though she said the final 26km were a challenge after a missed water bottle."I think the the last two laps were pretty intense and pretty tough because the Spanish girl attacked at the feed zone and I didn't catch my bottle there, so I rode like two laps without my bottle," she said at the post-race press conference. "That was hard because I got pretty bad cramps. But I think I worked really on my mental strength, and that just kept going. I'm not the best sprinter, but I just try to to sprint as best as I can."This year's route for the junior women measured 5.6km longer than the Kigali route and included a little more climbing, a total of 1,614 metres of elevation gain. Canada, Great Britain and Spain came with five riders each, giving them an edge with numbers.It was not until the second lap that the complexion of the peloton began to change, with riders falling off the back rather than anyone accelerating away. Spain, Australia and Poland were represented at the front.With just under 45km to go, French rider Sidonie Vachet put a spark in the proceedings with an attack at the front of a fractured peloton. She opened a slight 16-second gap on the uphill to start a fourth circuit, marking the halfway point of the 80.4km race.Behind, Scout Wellmeier (USA) rode at the front with Lluna Jimenez (Spain), Eva Drhova (Czechia), the Australian duo Chloe Bowen and Neve Parslow, and Polish duo Maria Okrucińska and Amelia Szymańska, and another 31 riders packed into the peloton.Bright sunshine helped the temperatures rise as high as 24°C (76°F), the warmest afternoon of the championships so far, and riders took on plenty of liquids at the feed zone along the climb. Across the summit of the Camillien-Houde, Vachet relented to the pace behind and the race reset.Once across the Polytechnique climb and on the twisting city-centre streets of Montréal, Great Britain riders could be seen gathering at the front. But it was an acceleration from Colombia's Zara Sofia Lamprea that came on the approach to the Parc Avenue climb.Lamprea carried a 10-second advantage, with Wellmeier trailing in solo second. The reduced peloton of 35 riders began the chase with two laps remaining at 20 seconds.There was a crash at the front of the race under a heavy canopy of trees, with Lamprea and Wellmeier going down. Both were back riding quickly, but as they made the penultimate ascent of Camillien-Houde, the chase began closing down their effort.A group of 10 crested the summit, and Lamprea just a few seconds behind and Wellmeier farther back, now chasers. France, Spain and Germany each had two riders, with one rider each from the USA, Netherlands, Great Britain and Switzerland. Then on the back side of Mont Royal, more riders tagged along for a bigger group.Riders upped the pace to position at the front, passing crowds at the Polytechnique Montréal centre for science and technology, with a series of twisting turns on the descent causing riders to go wide on the course.With 18.5km to go, Nabyenka García (Mexico) was the next rider to put in an extra effort, gapping the field by 15 seconds quickly on a flatter section. The Mexican rider looked back several times, and finally kept on the accelerator to go alone.The bell lap rang with long shadows forming in the late Canadian afternoon, García still out front but only by 14 seconds. The curse of race leaders continued as she stopped for a mechanical, looking to reposition her chain, and was forced back in the peloton.Wellmeier, Vachet, Parslow, Orucińska and Lidia Castro (Spain) were setting the pace at the bottom of the final ascent. Mirthe Mons (Netherlands) pushed the pace at the front, which seemed to spur others to give it a go. Soon a trio were at the front - Anja Grossmann (Switzerland), Alejandra Neira (Spain) and Matilde Rossignoli (Italy) - and with 10km to go had 20 seconds on Okrucińska and Mons.With 4km to go, the trio weren't showing signs of working togehter, which allowed Mons and Okrucińska, the new world time trial champion, to edge closer in the chase. "Maybe we should have worked a little bit more together, so the other two wouldn't came back. But that's junior racing because junior racing is always a little bit more hectic and a little bit more without a clear tactic. I wanted to work together, but it was not my decision," Grossmann said later.With 2km to go, there were five to fight for three medals.Mons struck first on the final climb. Then mountain bike world champion Grossman passed, then Rossignoli, but it was Neira who went wide on the right side and took the victory.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Subscribers get unlimited access to exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go! item.title: How to watch Yankees vs. Red Sox in AL Wild Card Series: Start times, channels, and more
item.author: Dani Mohr
item.content:encoded: The MLB postseason is finally upon us, and the No. 4 seed Yankees are kicking things off by facing the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, just as they did in 2025. New York will end the season at least four games better than Boston, but as they say, all records reset to 0-0 come October — or very-late September in the case of the 2026 season.The Red Sox defeated the Cubs on Friday afternoon to officially clinch the No. 5 seed, meaning the Yankees will have home-field advantage by starting the postseason in the Bronx. They already knew they would be hosting, but it wasn’t yet official that they would face Boston. Per MLB’s Sarah Langs, this will be the seventh all-time postseason meeting between the Yanks and Red Sox, tied for the second-most common matchup in league history and trailing only the 12 famous Yankees/Dodgers World Series rumbles. New York and Boston have each won three series apiece in the playoff head-to-heads.You won’t want to miss all the action in the best-of-three series next week, with the winner advancing to face the Rays in the American League Division Series in a race for the pennant.Here’s all the information you’ll need to know to tune into every game this weekend. This post will be updated with first pitch times as soon as they are announced, though given the hubbub that usually surrounds Yankees/Red Sox, it would be a surprise if they weren’t all night games.How to watch Yankees vs. Red Sox in Wild Card Series Tuesday, September 29 TBD: NBCPeacock Wednesday, September 30 TBD: NBCPeacock Thursday, October 1 TBD: NBCPeacock

item.title: 'We gave it everything' - Aubin Sparfel ready to join Paul Seixas at Decathlon CMA CGM after Montreal Worlds disappointment
item.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
item.content:encoded: Rising talent Aubin Sparfel ends his under-23 career in disappointment, having finished just off the podium in fourth place in the under-23 men's race at the UCI Road World Championships on Friday.The 20-year-old French rider came into the race as the big favourite, and was hoping to secure the rainbow jersey. Now, he will turn his attention to joining compatriot Paul Seixas in the WorldTour with Decathlon CMA CGM after spending four seasons growing through the team's development ranks. "We are a little bit disappointed, but we gave it everything," Sparfel told "Of course, we were here for the victory. It's like that. I'm super proud of the team and proud of myself. I had a super amount of pressure on me after the win last week [Grand Prix de Wallonie], and I felt like I could finally dream about winning."Sparfel had another successful season with the Decathlon CMA CGM Development programme, kicking off the year with an overall victory at Le Tour de Bretagne Cycliste, taking sixth overall at Boucles de la Mayenne-Crédit Mutuel, fourth overall at Giro d'Italia Next Gen, and winning a stage of the Tour de l'Avenir. He capped off his season with a victory at the one-day Lotto Grand Prix de Wallonie, showing top form heading into these Worlds and setting himself up as one of the favourites."Of course, I learned a lot this year. I won a lot, and I think I'm ready to step up. It was a super good season, and I can thank everyone around me. My team, the France team, my coaches and my family. It was a super good year," he said.During the under-23 men's road race, Sparfel joined a chase group that also included silver medallist Héctor Álvarez (Spain) and bronze medallist Jesper Stiansen (Norway) in a failed effort to bring back new world champion Ashlin Barry (USA).Despite his disappointment in finishing fourth, Sparfel praised Barry on his winning performance. "Ashlin was super strong," Sparfel told . "We knew that he could win this year, but we did everything we could as a team, and we were super strong as a team. "In the last two laps we did a lot with the other guys from the big favourites, but in the end, we arrived in the race for second place - it's like that."Sparfel will now turn his attention to racing alongside Seixas, fourth overall in the Tour de France this year and a favourite in the elite men's road race on Sunday. The two riders are among the nation's most promising talents on the WorldTour."I will go to the WorldTour, so I will no longer race in the under-23s. I've ridden on every team with Paul since we were juniors and know him really well," Sparfel told ."I will race for Decathlon next season, and we will see what we can do. I will speak with the team about my race program, but I'm proud of my under-23 racing season, and now I will focus on elite for next season."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: New York Yankees vs. Baltimore Orioles: Brendan Beck vs. Trevor Rogers
item.author: Matt Ferenchick
item.content:encoded: Expected inclement weather of Saturday led to the Yankees and Orioles moving around their weekend regular season finale and playing two games today on Friday. Today’s opener will feature the CC Sabathia number retirement ceremony that was originally set for tomorrow. After that pomp and circumstance, the Yankees and O’s will get their three game set going.In the first of today’s games, the Yankees will give the start to Brendan Beck, who was just called up alongside Yerry De los Santos with Luis Gil and Bradley Hanner farmed out last night. So far, Beck has made three MLB appearances since debuting earlier this season. He has an 8.22 ERA in 7.2 innings, including five runs allowed in 3.2 innings back on July 4th, which was his first career MLB start. Between the playoffs coming up and today now being a doubleheader, the Yankees more than anything will be hoping he can soak up some innings.Backing up him, the Yankees will be running out their lefty lineup, sending out Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario. Ali Sánchez will be behind the plate before switching with Austin Wells for the nightcap.With the lefty lineup starting, the Yankees will be facing, as you might guess, a lefty. Trevor Rogers will be going for Baltimore. He has a 4.07 ERA in 165.2 innings this season. This could be his last start with the Orioles after a very up-and-down tenure that began at the 2024 Trade Deadline, as he is a free agent at season’s end.We hope that you’ll come join us in the game thread for all of today’s action, so here’s how to watch the opener today.: Yankee Stadium – Bronx, NY: 4:05 p.m. ET: YES (NYY) | MASN (BAL): WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 (NYY) | 98 Rock 97.9 FM, WBAL 1090 AM (BAL) Gotham Sports App, MLB.tv (out-of-market only)

item.title: 'Once I got away, I just committed' - Ashlin Barry never hit the wall, got caught or stumbled on march to first gold medal at Road Worlds
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: With 1.7km to go in the men's under-23 road race at the 2026 Road World Championships, the USA's Ashlin Barry was riding solo on one of the few flat roads on the Montréal circuit when a TV camera captured him shaking his head, seeming to realise he would soon have a gold medal for a birthday present."I don't know how I did that," he said after receiving his gold medal and rainbow jersey.Going into the 174.2km contest, Barry had expected it to be the usual frenzy of high-octane racing among the field of 170-plus riders. He only wanted to stay away from the "uncontrolled" racing and find an opportunity if it was there."It was a hard start, and there's attacks going [everywhere]. I didn't really script it going in. I had maybe an idea of what I could do."I didn't think I'd be strong enough to follow the best guys on the climbs. So I just thought if I could get ahead, then maybe that would give me some room to go on the climb and still make the front group. Once I was away, I just committed."Honestly, I didn't think I could do it until the last lap, when I reached the top of the last climb. I attacked early in the race because I was worried I wouldn’t be able to follow the better climbers on the climb. In the end, I managed to keep everyone behind me. It feels surreal," the birthday boy, who turned 19 on Friday, admitted.He saw the gap times posted on the bulletin board from the moto on his two-lap charge with Kristian Egholm (Denmark), both getting away as part of a five-rider break on the fourth of 13 laps as the Dane was the only rider able to stay with Barry.The reigning US Pro men's U23 road champion then struck out on his solo escape with just under 29km to go, a full two laps of focus. That was the moment he saw an opportunity, but still wasn't confident."I kept seeing the gap and kept expecting it to come down on the climbs. Somehow, I was able to hold it. I was kind of just riding my pace and expecting some riders would come across to me. You know, so I just tried not to overextend or go over my limit, and I just kept pushing and eating and drinking as much as possible. "I thought, eventually, I'd get caught or kind of hit a wall, and somehow it never happened. I really just rode my own pace and went as fast as I could to the finish. The last two laps I just gave it everything I had."Barry finished fourth in the U23 time trial earlier this week, and thought he had a chance at a medal there. He said an unexpected bonus from training for several weeks on his TT bike seemed to help the most in the road race."I thought the TT would be a really big opportunity for me, so I was really focusing on it in my training. And in the end, that probably helped quite a bit in the road race. I think between the hills, I was just able to stay really efficient and conserve energy well. So definitely could have made the difference in the end." This is his third World Championships medal after claiming silvers as a junior in the time trial and the on the track in the Omnium. However, it was special not just because of the colour, but where he won. The teenager lives with his family in Toronto, a dual citizen of US and Canada, and he opted to ride for Team USA two years ago for the best resources.His immediate family was in attendance - father Michael Barry of Canada, mother Dede Demet-Barry of USA, his sister Holland, and his dog. Both of his parents are retired professional cyclists, with Demet-Barry the other family member to have won a race in Montreal, doing so at the women's World Cup road race in 2002, finishing on top of Mount Royal. Besides an extended celebration of his birthday tonight with family and friends, Barry already had sights on 2027 and beyond, wearing his new rainbow stripes as a U23 rider next year on the road, and perhaps getting an early call from the Visma-Lease a Bike development team to the WorldTour squad. "I have a contract to join the WorldTour team with Visma, I don't know if that'll be next year or the year after. You know, on paper I was supposed to have two years in the development team, so we'll see. I think it'd be cool to race in the World Championship jersey, do some U23 races next year. But if they think I'm ready to step up and go to the World Tour, then that would be pretty cool too."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: The surprise ex-F1 driver aiding Alpine's revival
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: Alpine has revealed a surprise asset supporting its Formula 1 revival this season - ex-Red Bull driver and podium finisher Daniil Kvyat.Kvyat, who started 110 grands prix from 2014 to 2020, quietly rejoined the Enstone team this year as a simulator driver.He had a stint at Alpine in 2021 as its reserve driver, having spent his F1 career racing for Red Bull's teams across multiple stints split by a year on the sidelines in 2018, when he was a simulator driver for Ferrari.Kvyat's role has been kept under wraps as he shares simulator duties with Alpine reserve drivers Paul Aron and Kush Maini.This includes development work but also race weekend support duties when Aron is required to be on-site at flyaway races.During race weekends, Kvyat keeps in contact with Alpine race driver Pierre Gasly, who he was team-mate to at Red Bull's junior team and has a good relationship with, to share direct feedback.Kvyat is understood to have played a significant role in Alpine's in-weekend turnarounds in Japan and Canada.Alpine is enjoying a much improved season in F1 as the new rules and its switch to Mercedes engines have launched it back to the head of the midfield.Kvyat has raced and/or tested NASCAR, top-level sportscar and Formula E machinery since his F1 exit, and had a role as a reference driver racing against an autonomous vehicle in Abu Dhabi.He is competing in Japan's Super GT series this year in the GT300 category, alongside veteran driver Takashi Kogure. The pair are 16th in the points with a best class finish of sixth.

item.title: Gary Anderson: Breaking down Audi's colossal F1 upgrade
item.author: Gary Anderson
item.content:encoded: Audi should get the prize for the most comprehensive car update this season given how many new parts it has brought to Azerbaijan. However, it’s all about how it works together - and not just about a jumble of parts.Starting as always with the front wing, it looks like a completely new package. The mainplane now has a more defined upsweep going outboard, still integrated into the footplate of the front wing endplate, while the flap assembly appears to be loaded further inboard.Both of these changes will improve the consistency of the airflow going around the inside of the front tyre, especially when varying degrees of steering lock are applied.The increase in the three-dimensional effect on the leading edge of the front wing endplate will increase the outwash, as will the reduction in the camber of the blue-highlighted horizontal vane coming out of that endplate and the increase in size and detail of the small orange vane just in front of the tyre.Audi is more or less alone in that its front wing actuator is mounted on the wing’s upper surface. As opposed to hiding it, Audi has decreased its size.All of these developments could be grouped together as one development to better manage the airflow going around the inside and outside of the front tyre and wheel assembly.F1 being an open-wheel formula, the tyres are one of the most obtrusive blockages that F1 teams have to aerodynamically deal with. Changes in this area can have consequences further downstream, so these changes have led Audi into a very comprehensive update package.Audi's unique (until McLaren introduced its new sidepod package) sidepod leading edge and radiator inlet have also been modified in that there is now a slightly more bulbous section at the floor leading edge. This is probably to be more sympathetic to the airflow as it separates to go under the floor’s leading edge and/or around the side of the floor.The actual sidepods have also changed, with the upper surface now allowing more downwash and, with that, a change to the cooling exit system. Audi has gone from an array of louvres to a more common opening. This has required the magenta-highlighted section to be made into two sections: the front part with an opening at the rear and the rear section’s leading edge blocked off, which looks very bulbous.Continuing that theme of managing the airflow around the front tyres, the next question is - how can you optimise that new and revised flow structure? This magenta-highlighted outer floor edge doesn’t look very different. There seems to be a small more aggressive turned-up section just behind the bargeboard area; it’s simply a knife edge which should, because of the difference in pressure on the top and bottom surfaces, produce a vortex along its length, helping to seal that area of the floor.To complete this floor detail, Audi has also revisited the vanes in front of the rear tyre contact patch. This is in line with what I said earlier about managing the airflow around the blockage created by the tyres. Maximising the outwash in this area means there is less inwash, which disrupts the airflow structure to the diffuser, reducing its efficiency.Small details also count, as they all add up. This area of the intersection between the halo and the leading edge of the headrest can very easily create turbulence that affects the stability of the driver’s head. This small vane will help to consistently manage some of that turbulence.There are now four fairly large cooling exit openings. The cooling system works because of the pressure drop across the radiator cores: positive pressure on the inlet, negative pressure on the outlet. It’s very difficult to increase the positive pressure as that is generated by car speed, but a larger, better-positioned opening can fairly easily increase the negative pressure at the exit. The important thing is to minimise the downforce losses that any of these openings induce.Audi has also changed the angle of support that the diffuser sides are getting from these longer and repositioned floor stays that are highlighted in green.Nothing has been left unaddressed. The rear wing trailing edge trim details have also come under review. The aero, as with the cooling exits, is in reality circuit-dependent, so depending on the circuit requirements it can be altered as the race weekend progresses.The battle in that midfield is just as intense, if not more so, than the battle up front. Every single point has potential $ signs in front of it.Alpine introduced its big upgrade a few races ago, Williams came to Baku with a big upgrade, mainly a weight reduction - and now it’s Audi’s turn to air its developments. Who has taken the biggest step?Hopefully we will get an indication this weekend. Audi has not fared well so far - but Baku is a strange circuit.

item.title: UCI Road World Championships: Ashlin Barry powers to under-23 men's title with 30-kilometre solo attack
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Ashlin Barry (USA) claimed the country's first ever under-23 road race title in the UCI Road World Championships, pulling off an audacious 30-kilometre solo attack from a five-rider breakaway that had already been off the front for more than 100 kilometres.Barry said he only went on the attack to get ahead and save some energy on the climbs for when the attacks came from the strongest riders."I didn't really think I would be strong enough to follow the the best guys on the climbs. Once I was away, I just committed. Honestly, I didn't think I could do it until until the last lap when I reached the top of the last climb. "Just complete disbelief, honestly."It was a massive birthday present for the dual Canadian-American citizen - the son of former pros Michael Barry and Dede Demet-Barry - who turned 19 today and was the eighth-youngest rider in the field. He gave North America something to celebrate after the region had been shut out of the under-23 men's medals since Taylor Phinney (USA) tied Canadian Guillaume Boivin for the bronze in 2010.Smiling for the cameras and waving to the crowds as he climbed to the finish, Barry crossed the line with his chasers well out of sight. It was 53 seconds before Hector Alvarez (Spain) out-sprinted the remnants of the breakaway for the silver, banging his bars in frustration, while Jesper Stiansen (Norway) took home the bronze.Barry lives in Toronto, and had ample support around the course as both the host country and the US fans who travelled to Montreal were cheering him on as he worked to hold off his chasers."It was just unreal being out there, seeing so many so many friends, seeing my family. I could hear my dog barking on the side of the course," Barry said. "It really felt like a home race out there. I just have to say I'm like so so grateful for for the support I had, and yeah, there's just so many people I have to have to thank."The result exceeded his expectations for his home Worlds, especially after he finished off the podium in the time trial."Honestly, I didn't didn't think it was possible," Barry said. "I thought maybe at best I could get get a medal or something or a nice result. I thought maybe in the TT - I could have a chance, but to to win on this course is just unbelievable."For Álvarez, third in the time trial, it was a difficult pill to swallow missing out on another world title."Ashlin was just stronger," the Spaniard said. "It was only me and the group against him, he was super strong and I need to congratulate him."I wanted to arrive at the front, but I have two [medals] - not the one I was coming for... but I am happy, in any event."Stiansen, however, was happy to reach his goal of landing on the podium."It was a crazy hard sprint and also a hard race - to come with third place is amazing. It was our goal today, but to do it, it's never easy," he said."It was full guys all day and crazy chaotic. Luckily, I found my legs during the last lap, so I could attack up to the front group, and I'm super happy to end it off with the third place."The under-23 men lined up under sunny skies ready to take on 13 laps of a 13.4km circuit for a total of 174.2km and 3,497m of elevation. The circuit started on the Avenue du Parc and include two main climbs: Camillien-Houde to the top of Mount Royal, Côte de la Polytechnique, and then tackle the uphill drag to the finish back on Avenue du Parc.Frank Ragilo (Estonia) made the first move early in the opening lap as the sun was just peaking above the skyscrapers of downtown Montreal. He was joined by Mads Landbo (Denmark), Filip Durdyk (Poland) and a rider each from Spain and the USA but the breakaway only gained ten seconds and was brought back before the end of the lap. There was plenty of action at the back, with riders getting tailed off, touching wheels and falling, or suffering mechanicals. Ben Wiggins (Great Britain) was forced to chase back on, too.Before the end of the first lap, Kristian Egholm (Denmark) followed his teammate's lead and attacked, pulling away with Viktor Soenens (Belgium) and William Heffernan (Australia), with Romet Pajur (Estonia) trying to bridge. Before the end of the lap, the breakaway had swelled to 13 riders with Enea Sambinello (Italy), Pierre Basset (France), Timothee Coudiere Cantin (France), Landbo, William Holmes (Australia), Halvor Dolven (Norway), Jaider Muñoz (Colombia), Dawid Lewandowski (Poland), Mil Morang (Luxembourg) and Alejandro Granados (Costa Rica). They were chased by Enaut Urcaregui (Spain) and Jaka Marolt (Slovenia) at 13 seconds, and the majority of the peloton at 50 seconds at the end of lap 2.When a powerful chasing group set off in pursuit, with Cameron Rogers (Australia), Noah Andersen (Denmark), Victor Loulergue and Ugo Fabries (France), Jasper Schoofs (Belgium), David Haverdings and Guus van den Eijnden (Netherlands), Samuel Novak (Slovakia), Ashlin Barry (USA), Ben Wiggins (Great Britain) and Patryk Goszczurny (Poland), the peloton quickly shut it down, and the race was all back together on the fourth lap.An attack then came from Samuel Novak (Slovakia), with William Heffernan (Australia) bridging across along with Mattie Dodd (Great Britain), Kristian Egholm (Denmark) and Ashlin Barry (USA).By the end of the sixth lap, the five riders had pushed their lead out to just over two minutes, but an attack from Dodd at the start of the seventh lap with 75km remaining, saw him go clear of the group and force a chase from Heffernan, Novák and Barry, completely distancing Egholm from the breakaway.The efforts were short lived and the quintet reconnected before the start of the eighth lap but their lack of cooperation had reduced the gap to 1:45.By the time they reached the ninth lap, a six rider chase group broke off the front of the field that included Matteo Scalco (Italy), Rémi Arsac (France), Matteo Van Huffel (Belgium), Max Brok (Germany), Jacob Bush (Great Britain) and Jack Ward (Australia) and were in pursuit.Egholm found his second wind and surged on the Camillien-Houde ascent with Barry bridging the gap. The pair gained a slim seven seconds on Dodd, Heffernan and Novák. However the remnants of that original breakaway were reabsorbed into a larger selection of 25 riders that formed behind, leaving Egholm and Barry out front with a 45-second advantage.With riders from Belgium and Switzerland setting the pace, the gap to the two breakaway riders was slashed to just 30 seconds with 30km to go. Barry took his chances and surged distancing himself from Egholm.With two laps remaining, Barry pushed on in front of a chase group of five: Matisse van Kerckhove (Belgium), Hector Alvarez (Spain) Guus van den Eijnden (Netherlands), and Cameron Rogers (Australia), with Egholm tucking in behind them. At the bell, Barry still held out hope with his gap hovering at 40 seconds over the quintet and 1:08 on the larger peloton.As his rivals behind began to look at each other to chase, Barry just kept powering ahead and only extended his lead to win the gold medal.Ashlin Barry (United States)Erazem Valjavec (Slovenia)Daan Dijkman (Netherlands)Marcis Shelton (United States)Bogdan Zabelinskiy item.title: SD Worx-Protime add more strength to their climbing roster with Axelle Dubau-Prévot
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: After four riders announced their departure in recent weeks, SD Worx-Protime are ramping up their recruitment with Axelle Dubau-Prévôt heading to the Dutch team in 2027.Though the 30-year-old Dubau-Prévôt only has one season riding at WorldTour level, and only returned to the road in 2025, she has competed in cyclocross, mountain bike and gravel, bagging top results in the latter discipline. She rode with some success on the road as a junior, then spent the 2017 and 2018 seasons riding at Continental level for Spanish and Belgian teams. Despite this, her 2026 season was hugely successful, with 10th place at Liège-Bastogne-Liège as her outstanding result on the road. In gravel races this year, she has plenty of top-10 placings, with third at the European Championships her most notable result."We are convinced that Axelle still has plenty of room for improvement," the team’s sporting director Danny Stam said, admitting they have been following her since the UAE Tour in February.“Precisely because we want to strengthen our squad for the Ardennes classics, she’s an excellent fit for us. As she had to ride many races in support of the team last season, we haven’t yet seen the best of her. There’s certainly still room for improvement when it comes to climbing.”Dubau-Prévôt admitted she is still new to the sport, saying, "It wasn’t until 2026 that I turned fully professional for the first time. Before that, I combined cycling with my job as a nutritionist. I knew I had talent, but I thought, ‘What if I went all out for it?’"After Liège-Bastogne-Liège, I got calls from several teams. I took a chance with Team SD Worx-Protime. I’ve been following this team for years. It’s a dream to now be part of it. It feels a bit bizarre: ten years ago, my career was more or less over, and now, in my thirties, I’m suddenly a member of one of the best cycling teams in the world."Dubau-Prévôt, the sister of 2025 Tour de France Femmes champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, is the fourth rider to sign with SD Worx this year, balancing their losses, and joins Kerbaol, Eline Jansen and Rachele Barbieri.Leaving the team are Marta Lach, Blanka Vas, Femke Markus and Julia Kopecký, while Elena Cecchini will retire after 15 years as a professional.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: What explains Mercedes' most dominant performance of 2026
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: George Russell's pole-winning margin at Formula 1's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, 0.837 seconds, marked the biggest defeat for Mercedes' rivals in a 2026 qualifying session.Even with just one car in Q3, Mercedes managed to beat its previous benchmark, of 0.785s, from the season-opening Australian GP weekend.It undeniably has the best car and power unit package in Baku, but its rivals compromised themselves, making that gap bigger than it needed to be, as we explain.Verstappen was down on powerMax Verstappen's Red Bull topped final practice and was looking like Mercedes’ closest challenger ahead of - and during - qualifying.But that challenge failed to materialise, with Verstappen ending up eighth and a second and a half away from pole - his biggest time gap to pole of the season when he has set a lap in Q3.His returning team-mate Isack Hadjar ended up as the lead Red Bull, in fourth, over half a second clear of Verstappen, who believed the majority of the gap could be explained by a mysterious power issue."The whole qualifying we were down on power, it was consistently half a second down to Isack's car," Verstappen said after qualifying."For whatever reason, we don't know why that happened in qualifying. Then in Q3, the middle lap coming out of the last corner, my battery didn't go to 100%, so I had to abort that lap."And too cold tyres then, because you don't have the speed, you don't have the power that you should have. Then when I tried on my final lap, with no power, the tyres [being] too cold and a yellow flag, it's not happening."Verstappen encountered the yellow flags for Lando Norris's off in Q3, which also compromised him, so that 1.5s gap was far from representative.If Verstappen had been able to put his three best sectors together, that deficit would have been 1.014s. That gap would have been reduced further with a clean final Q3 lap, with Lewis Hamilton believing Red Bull has the second-fastest car in Baku."It's a shame...the whole weekend we're doing a good job, I'm happy with the car and then it all just falls apart in qualifying because of problems out of my control," Verstappen said."It's a little bit this season...it's a bit too fragile at times."The Red Bull drivers have suffered from an aerodynamic degradation issue all season but Verstappen said this wasn't present in Baku.Asked by The Race if he might sacrifice his eighth place on the grid to take a new power unit, Verstappen said: "First just need to figure out what it is [the problem]."Otherwise, if you have to run with that also tomorrow [in the race], it's not going to be a lot of fun. Let's see."Verstappen did rank 20th out of 22 drivers in the speed trap (306.3km/h) across the start/finish line in qualifying, 11km/h down on Hadjar and over 18km/h down on Hamilton, the fastest driver through there.Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies confirmed Verstappen's comments, saying his car developed an issue during qualifying that "got worse as the session went on"."Not only did it bring a large straight-line speed deficit, but it also made our life very complicated with energy deployment and tyre preparation," said Mekies, who felt Verstappen's eighth place was "sort of a damage limitation" in the circumstances and added that Red Bull would "change the faulty parts" overnight.McLaren's major straightline deficitVerstappen wasn't the only driver complaining about straightline speed after qualifying.Reigning world champion Lando Norris seems resigned to a difficult Azerbaijan GP considering McLaren's overall lack of aerodynamic efficiency and what he perceives to be a particular straightline deficit on his car compared to the sister McLaren of Oscar Piastri."The guys say everything's working as expected, but when you see eight tenths to the top, it's painful," said Norris. "Our time losses are in the straights. That's another area we just need to look at, because we're just a step worse to Mercedes in everything straightline-related."I've been comfortable in the car the whole weekend. My last lap I made a mistake and I paid the price, but I'm at a point in the championship where I kind of have to go for pole, or I kind of die trying. Of course, I paid the price for pushing too much, but it is what it is.“It's been tough, especially with my car. We have to understand why I'm basically having to push more than Oscar to try and make up for my straightline speed [deficit].”Team principal Andrea Stella said McLaren was investigating Norris's deficit and added: "It seems to be linked to the behaviour of the fuel injection, something that hopefully we will be able to or the adaptive systems should be able to improve [for the race]."It looks occasionally [like] the power unit generates a bit less power. But this is a specific phenomenon; it's nothing to do with the overall behaviour of the power unit."McLaren has brought a significant suite of upgrades to Baku, in an attempt to improve the car's efficiency - including a return for its revolving rear 'H-wing' that debuted at Monza - but Norris clearly felt further steps are needed to put McLaren in range of Mercedes."They have a very efficient car - they always have done for years," he added. "We need to take a big step in that direction if we want to be competitive in any straightline speed track for the rest of the season."But they also have just a good car in all the corners as well. They're just doing a better job in all areas, power unit and car."Stella agreed. "While we have the same power unit, there's a few differences and I think it's fair to say that their package, chassis, ratios, power unit itself, it just seems to be more effective when it comes to generating top speed."Hamilton rues Ferrari run plan and 'stupid tyres'Hamilton's furious weaving before each of his push laps in Q3 highlighted that getting temperature into his front tyres was a factor in his challenge for a better grid slot falling away."I was weaving to try and save my life, and I still couldn't get these stupid tyres working," he said afterwards after he ended up sixth. "Such a pain in the ass. We've got to bring back some good tyres."But tyre temperatures did not explain the full deficit to pole position as he ended up 1.3s adrift of Russell and nearly half a second behind Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.Instead, the biggest time loss came from Hamilton having found himself running at the front of a train of cars so he was left without a slipstream.Ferrari opted to change its run plan for Q3, doing push, cool, push laps rather than having a run and then changing tyres.But its strategy backfired when cars Hamilton was running behind in the train - such as the two McLarens and Carlos Sainz's Williams - all were stopping, so got out of the way.By the time things had shaken out, Hamilton had realised he was alone on track, more than 25 seconds behind Russell and simply towing his team-mate Charles Leclerc around.At one point, realising what was happening, Hamilton asked his team for advice on what to do - but then told them not to worry as he would "look on the TV".Based on what Hamilton had learned when he got a good tow in FP3 as he ended up third, the lack of a slipstream was very costly."It was six tenths," he said, when The Race asked how much the gain from getting the tow right was worth. "I didn't have one in that session."Leclerc did, though, having followed Hamilton around, and that helped him secure his spot on the front row, albeit still well adrift of Russell.Russell’s first pole position since the Austrian GP in late-June stands as his most compelling qualifying performance since his outstanding Friday and Saturday at the Barcelona GP.He pointed to a slipstream that he felt gave him a tenth or two extra on a qualifying lap that "all perfectly came together" in Baku."I've been feeling in a great spot this whole weekend," said Russell. "I felt confident, I felt hooked up. I'm getting more and more on top of this car and what it requires, and it's just all feeling more intuitive."Not that he believed this has come from nowhere. Asked whether he felt this represented a breakthrough, he suggested that wasn't the case and instead pointed to his improved form since the summer break."It's definitely just been perfectly hooked up for me this weekend so far," he said. "Me and my team have put so much work in to help me get on top of the limitations."Since the summer break it's been great and the performance has been substantially better than the results have shown."Inevitably, Antonelli's absence from the track after clipping the inside wall at Turn 1 in Q1 means Russell didn't have the opportunity to prove he would have maintained his form from the build-up to qualifying and outpace his team-mate.But Antonelli, who completed fewer practice laps than anyone after a hydraulic problem struck in FP1, with the resulting power unit change delaying his start to FP2, always seemed on the back foot."I did miss a lot of laps but in FP3 I felt pretty good," said Antonelli. "It was just a misjudgement, with the grip changing so much. An unnecessary one in Q1, and it’s a very good reminder that, like this, things don't go my way, so I need to do a much better job."

item.title: What’s behind Norris’ top-speed issue in Baku – and why McLaren itself is down on Mercedes

item.title: 'Anything other than gold would be a disappointment' – Ultra-ambitious Paul Seixas throws down the gauntlet for Road World Championships title
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: Paul Seixas may only just have turned 20 this week, but the young Frenchman is already aiming for the biggest goal possible in the Road World Championships elite men's race on Sunday – and he will have an entire team at his disposal to help him achieve it.Second in the GP de Montréal less than a fortnight ago, and a surprise bronze medallist in the elite men's time trial last Sunday, Seixas spent no small amount of time in the French elite men team's press conference earlier this week weighing up the considerable strength in depth of the opposition. In terms of possible winning scenarios for Sunday, Seixas said he had been working specifically in training on his sprints, which he feels could well be necessary for him to succeed. However, as he also warned, any battle for the victory after 270 kilometres is a very different beast to how finishes tend to play out after shorter races than the Worlds. But with his team backing him 100%, he said, and some great form, his morale going into what is only his second elite men's road race this autumn – he was 13th in Kigali last year – could only be high.Asked if he needed to finish solo to win gold, Seixas explained that that might not be necessary, due to the inherent difficulty of such a hilly, long race, with nearly 4,000 metres of vertical climbing."It doesn't matter which rider you are, they'll all tell you they prefer to finish alone because it's the simplest way of winning," Seixas said in comments reported by ."But finishing with several riders on Sunday could actually help me. I'm not the slowest rider in the world and I've been working on that [his sprint] once a week. That helps me maintain my explosiveness which can be important."At the end of 270 kilometres of racing, it's never the same. The finish is hard and we'll have to see about the wind direction as well."When it comes to being in the best position possible to take advantage of whatever circumstances Sunday throws at him, Seixas agreed that he felt complimented regardless at being given the role of sole leader for France."I know that I am physically capable of keeping up with the best, and the team is aware of that too. Do I feel the pressure? A little, but that is normal."Our ambition is simple: we want to win that title. Given my form, anything other than gold would really be a disappointment."Although Seixas was unable to beat Isaac del Toro (Mexico) on exactly the same terrain in the GP de Montréal, he did not feel overly troubled by the prospect of a similar scenario playing out again. His main concern, he explained, was to do with the pace of the competition, and keeping it as high as possible."What suits me the best is for the racing to be made tough," he explained. "We'll see how we do that, but we haven't had the pre-race meeting yet. [French team coach] Thomas Voeckler always has some ideas in his head about those questions, and I'm waiting to see what they are." "In theory, the Belgians are the top favourites, with Wout van Aert and Remco Evenepoel. They have two really strong leaders for two different scenarios, so it'll be up to them to control the race from the gun. But we'll see what we can do to challenge them."Just as Tom Pidcock argued a little later in the week, Seixas felt that despite having such a similar course, the Worlds would not be the same kind of event as the GP de Montréal."The long approach road to the circuit" – around 110 kilometres of racing – "changes things, and so does the lower number of laps" – 12 in the Worlds, 16 in Montréal. "To define what kind of rider can win on it, you'll just have to see how the course actually plays out. It's very open."Seixas said he had shifted his focus since the Worlds time trial completely, even if the bronze medal he took there was an excellent memory, to be sure that he kept his eye on what is the main prize: Sunday's road race."That's how it should be. I did the time trial well, but I've moved onto something else," he said. "I trained well, I've done some endurance work and I'm ready for the road race. My TT medal doesn't change things enormously, the two races don't have anything in common, but it does show I'm in good form, and that I've kept that good form in the last few days. "That gives me some more confidence for Sunday, but it doesn't change things so much."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: 'One final opportunity to give it everything' – Ashleigh Moolman Pasio set to close out 17-year professional career with World Championships road race
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: South Africa's Ashleigh Moolman Pasio is gearing up for her last outing on the road as a professional, with Saturday's elite women's road race at the World Championships set to draw to a close her 17-year career.The very last dance of Moolman Pasio's career will be at the Gravel World Championships in Nannup, Australia next month, she confirmed in a blog post on Friday, but Montreal will be her final road race as a professional.Turning 41 in December, Moolman Pasio has been racing on the European UCI circuit since 2009, gaining her first UCI contract in 2010 with Lotto Ladies Team when she was 24, and she's been a stalwart of the peloton ever since then, for a long time one of the only African cyclists in the bunch.Her career has spanned nearly two decades, and she's extended it multiple times in the last few years: she originally laid out her intentions to retire in 2022, then at the end of 2024, but extended her contract with AG Insurance-Soudal to bring her to the end of 2026.But first, there's the matter of closing the curtain on her own racing career."The preparation has not been completely smooth. I have not raced as much as I would have liked during the second half of the season, but I have continued to find ways to challenge myself. Racing virtually has helped me grow stronger week by week, push beyond my comfort zone and enjoy the process of building towards one final goal on the road."So, one last time on the road, I have done everything I can to prepare. I have arrived here in good shape, confident in my form and ready to give this final road race one enormous shot. I want to race bravely. I want to empty the tank. Most of all, I want to cross that finish line knowing that I gave everything I had, with no regrets."On Saturday, she will form part of a four-rider South Africa team, alongside Hayley Preen, Tiffany Keep and Lisa Bone. In some years, she has been South Africa's sole representative at the World Championships, but will line up alongside her compatriots this year, as well as riders from Mauritius, Zimbabwe, Eritrea, Rwanda and multiple other African nations."My racing journey will not be completely over - there is still one final adventure awaiting me at the Gravel World Championships - but Montreal will close an enormous and defining chapter of my life," she wrote."Then, I will be ready to move into the next one: using everything this sport has taught me to help pave the way for the next generation of African cyclists. To share my experience, knowledge and belief with young riders who may not yet realise what is possible - just as I once could not imagine what was possible for me."Moolman Pasio's career highlightsTwo-time Giro d'Italia runner-upFourth on the Tourmalet at the 2023 Tour de France GC wins at the Tour de Romandie and Emakumeen Bira12-time South African Champion (road race and time trial)Five-time African ChampionEighth at World Championships In her blog post, she shared various anecdotes and stories from her career, including the holiday with her now-husband Carl where he became convinced she could be one of the world's finest cyclists, and the decision to leave the world of study and engineering to pursue a career in the sport."After graduating, we took an enormous leap of faith and moved to Europe so I could try to build a professional cycling career. I could never have imagined where that decision would lead," she wrote."I never dreamt that I would compete at four Olympic Games, win mountain stages of the Giro, stand on the Giro podium multiple times, finish on the podium at Flèche Wallonne, win Emakumeen Bira and the Tour de Romandie, or become the first UCI Cycling Esports World Champion during the pandemic. I certainly never imagined that I would spend 17 years racing among the very best cyclists in the world."She also reflected on how her career has changed and evolved over the years, such as taking more interest in virtual racing during the pandemic, setting up the Rocacorba Collective and its ambitions to empower female riders, the biggest lessons of her career, and recovering from a broken back in 2024."Seventeen years ago, I arrived in Europe with a dream that initially felt far too big," she wrote. "Now, as I prepare to pin on a number for my final road race, I can look back with immense pride and gratitude. Not only for the results, but for the person this journey has helped me become, for the people who have walked it with me and for the community that will remain long after the racing ends."One last race on the road. One final opportunity to give it everything. No regrets."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Sainz penalised for second yellow flag breach in one day
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Williams Formula 1 driver Carlos Sainz has received a five-place grid penalty for ignoring yellow flags during Azerbaijan Grand Prix qualifying.The penalty denies Williams what was set to be its best grid position of the year, superseding Alex Albon's 11th place on the Monaco GP grid.Remarkably, the sanction came on a day on which Sainz was already investigated - and found guilty - of a different yellow-flag breach, although on that occasion he was let off with a reprimand due to mitigating circumstances.Sainz and Williams were originally hauled in front of the stewards after Friday morning practice for a yellow flag breach through Turn 4. The stewards ruled that Sainz "failed to sufficiently reduce speed" under the yellow flag - but felt there was sufficient mitigation to avoid the imposition of the grid penalty in "the very short period between the single yellow being displayed and Sainz entering the relevant marshalling sector".No such mitigation was present in a different incident, recorded during the third qualifying segment. In fact, the stewards pointed out that Sainz received advanced warning from the team that a yellow flag was out on the approach to Turn 3, and simply failed to heed it sufficiently.The warning in question was "yellow ahead, yellow ahead, [Lando] Norris, just do a lift, do a lift, and complete the lap" and then an apparent "clear-clear" that followed seconds later - seemingly creating a situation that led Sainz to believe the yellow flag was no longer acutely relevant."[Sainz] explained that he intended to demonstrate a reduction in speed across the yellow area as a whole," the stewards wrote as part of a lengthy explanation."He stated that he did not consider it necessary to reduce speed on the straight and instead intended to demonstrate his response when approaching and exiting Turn 3. He considered this to be a 'global lift' covering the consecutive yellow sectors. He further explained that the car [Norris] which had originally caused the yellow was no longer in the runoff area and that he expected the yellow flags to be withdrawn."The stewards did not accept this interpretation. Where consecutive marshalling sectors are subject to yellow-flag conditions, a driver must demonstrate a significant reaction to reduce speed in each individual yellow marshalling sector. A reduction in a subsequent sector cannot retrospectively satisfy the requirement applicable to the preceding yellow sector. The obligation is also not dependent on the driver's own assessment of whether the original hazard remains present within a particular part of the yellow sector."McLaren driver Lando Norris had indeed vacated the relevant runoff by that point - but as the FIA stewards do not want the drivers to self-assess the validity of a yellow flag, they found the lack of any "meaningful reduction in speed" in the relevant marshalling sector was sufficient grounds for the penalty.In addition to the five-position penalty, which demotes Sainz from ninth to 14th, he has also received two penalty points - taking him to a total of four for the 12-month period.Sainz was not alone in incurring a grid penalty after Baku qualifying.A three-position penalty has been assessed against Cadillac driver Sergio Perez for impeding McLaren driver Oscar Piastri in the opening segment.The stewards wrote that Perez "received two radio warnings" from the team but still forced a needless lift from the McLaren driver through the Turns 18-19-20 section, by "not managing his preparation lap in accordance with specific traffic-management instructions" - namely the race director's order that a driver on a prep lap stay to the right-hand side and avoid weaving in front of incoming cars.Because of the engine component penalties to the Aston Martin cars, however, Perez is only set to lose one position on the grid - going from 19th to 20th (the position he originally qualified in), behind team-mate Valtteri Bottas.

item.title: Verstappen reveals why Red Bull's engine problem in Baku was different than it seemed
Russell takes pole in Baku as Antonelli hits wall
item.content:encoded: George Russell takes pole position for Mercedes at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as his team-mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli crashes out.

item.title: Winners and losers from F1 Azerbaijan GP qualifying
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: As a headline statistic, the biggest pole position margin yet around the streets of Baku points to an Azerbaijan Grand Prix qualifying session that might've lacked a bit of edge.The reality was very different - and not just because of the contrasting fortunes of the two Mercedes drivers.Here's our pick of winners and losers from Friday:Loser: Kimi Antonelli (16th)Given Mercedes' form so far this weekend, even with how compromised Antonelli's Thursday had proven this was still an easy (relatively speaking) 18 points just begging to be collected.That's still a plausible outcome, but it sure will be harder now after an "unnecessary" impact with the inside barrier at Turn 1 during the opening segment."I had a lot more headwind compared to the lap before, so the front just was much stronger, and I turned in roughly in the same spot, but obviously the car turned more and I clipped the wall," Antonelli explained.With 81 points in the pocket he can afford it - but there's no need to 'spend' a chunk of that margin this weekend. And maybe he won't - but he's put himself in a bit of a danger zone, in terms of grid position and the overtaking he will now need to do. Winner: George Russell (1st)Even before runaway championship leader Antonelli clipped the Turn 1 wall, Russell had been in formidable form. Without his team-mate for competition, that turned into pole position by a crushing margin of 0.837s.Russell described himself as feeling "hooked up" from the start of the weekend, and while Max Verstappen, who he described as "the biggest threat", was hindered by yellow flags and a worsening engine issue, Russell always looked on target for pole position.While it will take far more than one pole position, or even a victory on Saturday, to reignite his faded title chances, it's an important step in what Russell calls the "upward cycle" of improving his performances. Loser: Max Verstappen (8th)Max Verstappen reckoned he was losing half a second to Isack Hadjar because of an engine/power-related problem - and what was Verstappen's deficit to Hadjar in Q3? 0.581s.OK, you'd expect Verstappen (who topped FP3) to beat Hadjar with the half-second deficit removed, especially after Hadjar's three-race injury lay-off, and he might still have done had he not caught a yellow flag on his final run.On his second run prior to that, his battery didn't go to 100% for the run to the finish line, so that was another chance lost. Combined with the car's front-bottoming, which caused brake struggles, that meant a day that looked so promising turned into a nightmare for Verstappen. Winner: Isack Hadjar (4th)Ever a glass-half-empty driver in his time in F1 so far, Hadjar emphasised that with continuity instead of injury he would've "definitely" been on the front row here - instead missing out by 0.141s."Nothing outstanding," he added. But while a 2027 deal is already in his pocket it's certainly not a bad time to remind everyone, after three rounds of impressively workmanlike stand-in pace from Liam Lawson, that Hadjar has had serious speed this year.And he did admit he has been happy about how he's eased himself into this weekend, at a track that is just waiting to catch you out."I told myself it's mandatory not to touch the wall or anything. For a comeback, there's no point taking a lot of risks. So I was really driving a bit under the limit the whole weekend in that very tight section - I think I just did that natural step in Q3." Loser: Audi (17th and 18th)The two heavily-upgraded Audis had not impressed very much in practice - but even so, the double Q1 exit looks like an aberration.It's not just the power unit, Gabriel Bortoleto insisted."There were tracks like Monza where we were almost in Q3 and there are more straights than here. So I think it's something bigger that we need to understand," he said."I think it was better [earlier in the weekend], but still we were always on the edge of going out in Q1."The whole weekend we had no grip. If you don't have grip, you cannot go fast in the corners. If you don't go fast, you don't make a laptime. It's simple as that, and it's what other teams, when they go out in Q1, they probably say."Team-mate Nico Hulkenberg was more cheery, in relative terms, arguing his Q1 exit was "mostly because of circumstances", specifically a yellow flag and a lost tow. And neither he nor Bortoleto is suggesting the upgrade is misfiring - but certainly it's proving no game changer for Baku. Winner (then loser): Carlos Sainz (9th)Sainz put Williams into Q3 for the first time this year as its significant car upgrade excelled on debut - although Sainz felt the result was an overachievement.Alex Albon joined Sainz in Q2 as Williams escaped Q1 with both cars for the first time since July's British GP, which serves as evidence the FW48 is a more competitive beast in Baku.But Sainz (who does still face a yellow flag investigation) felt his ninth place was a result of Williams nailing its tyre usage and run plan, and "some serious laps on the limit" from himself, to end up a little higher than it would be on pace alone.He described the car as no different "in feel, just quicker" because it's lighter and has a bit more downforce - but the work done to achieve that has been immediately rewarded.Sainz admitted that getting a noticeable result felt pretty good for him, too, after a year spent toiling further down the midfield - and described the laps to achieve that as "the highest stress of the season" because of the challenge threading through the twists of sector two on a gusty day and low-grip track.What a shame, then, that a good deal of that good work was undone by a five-place grid drop for failing to slow for yellow flags. Loser: Esteban Ocon (14th)That aforementioned Hadjar lock-up in Q2 (on the right front, sending him into the Turn 15 escape road) had no real impact on his own qualifying - but did compound the misery of another French driver.Ocon had three tenths in hand over team-mate Ollie Bearman coming into their final run in Q2, but couldn't match Bearman with his first effort after returning to the track - compromised by what he described as a "gust of wind", which seemingly sent him onto the outside kerb at Turn 16."And then I did the same laptime, again, [before] arriving to Turn 15. I don't know who went off [Hadjar], but I had to back off on the exit to make sure that I was not going to get any penalty," he vented."I did exactly the same laptime. So yeah, I lost, what, three-four tenths? Unbelievable. You know, I just have no words. It's different race weekend, same s**t. It's always something going on, on my side, if it's either the car, if it's something else, now yellow flag, safety cars, whatever."But I don't deserve all the s**t that I have on my back at the moment. So I don't know, I might need to take a good shower." Winner: Alpine (7th & 10th)Alpine took full advantage of Antonelli's absence to get both cars into Q3 - a good day for any midfield team when the top teams usually hog eight of the 10 spots at the top of the order.Pierre Gasly managed to beat Max Verstappen - caveated by Verstappen's power issue, but still impressive - with his take being "great balance, great car, managed to get to Q3 pretty comfortably".Franco Colapinto had more of a struggle, and his off into the Turn 15 run-off, blamed on a flatspot, also cost Gasly on his final flying lap. Gasly reckoned sixth-place qualifier Lewis Hamilton was also there for the taking without that.A scruffy Q3, but it didn't matter, and Gasly's confident of keeping the rest of the 'midfield' behind. Loser: Sergio Perez (20th)The opportunity was there but, in the words of Perez, Cadillac "needed everything to go our way" to bag its first Q2 appearance.Everything did not go its way.Perez said Cadillac had the "wrong programme" in terms of how he and team-mate Valtteri Bottas prepared their laps. That went further awry when Bottas, who was due to provide the tow, was called to the weighbridge.Then Perez had his final lap wrecked by Fernando Alonso going up the escape road at the Turn 15 left-hander ahead of him (a chain of events that meant the Aston Martin outqualified the Cadillac). To add insult to injury, Perez has also been assessed a three-place grid penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri.The biggest shame is that we didn't get to see what Baku specialist Perez was capable of dragging out of the Cadillac. Because the form was there: 13th in FP2, 16th in FP3 - at the end of an eight-lap stint on the soft tyre on the latter occasion, too.The positive for Perez and Cadillac is that this wasn't competitive reality setting in. But not for the first time this season, they've probably been left frustrated by imperfections in their own execution. (To such an extent that a three-place grid drop for impeding Oscar Piastri doesn't make a great deal of difference.) Winner: Oscar Piastri (3rd)Although a front-row position was possible, as he was just one thousandth slower than Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, it was important for Piastri to get on top of McLaren team-mate Lando Norris after struggling in recent times.Piastri described it as "not an easy weekend" for McLaren, so felt third on the grid was "a really good result".Though he admitted that there have been some difficult laps amongst the good ones in Baku, overall he was encouraged with his own performance. "On a personal level, I feel we've been building up well," said Piastri. "I was pretty happy with my laps in Q3." Loser: Arvid Lindblad (15th)Racing Bulls's hopes of significant mid-weekend gains have not so far come to fruition - the car looked outmatched in qualifying relative to some of its usual opposition, and is at risk of a particularly bad points day on Saturday if the two Alpines ahead benefit from some classic Baku chaos.But while Lawson simply lamented the deficit on the straights, saying that Racing Bulls drivers are "trying to make up time that is not really there", for team-mate Lindblad such a quiet Q2 exit felt particularly sour."I'm a bit frustrated, more at myself than anything just because I feel that I didn't do something special like I normally do at the end of these qualifyings to put us in the final part," he regretted, admitting that his Thursday crash has compounded a shortage of confidence on braking."It's not been a good day, it's not been a good week. I just need to understand why I haven't been on it."

item.title: Shimano Breaks Pedal Compatibility, Canyon’s Handlebar Surprise, and Finding Ride Motivation | Velo Podcast
item.author: Josh Ross
